articles.title: South Africa’s Malben, Egypt’s Elaraby eye automotive components manufacturing partnership - Engineering News
articles.summary: South Africa’s Malben, Egypt’s Elaraby eye automotive components manufacturing partnership  Engineering News
articles.full_text:
Malben Engineering’s Luca Smargiasso and the Elaraby Group’s Mohamed A El Araby signed a MoU in Alamein on October 2, at a ceremony witnessed by dignitaries including South Africa’s Trade, Industry and Competition Minister Parks Tau and Egypt’s Investment and Foreign Trade Minister Dr Mohamed Farid Saleh.
South African automotive components manufacturer Malben Engineering has signed an agreement with Egypt’s Elaraby Group, opening the way for the possible creation of a new venture to manufacture automotive components in the North African country.
The memorandum of understanding was initialled on the sidelines of the Africa Automotive Investment Forum, which took place in Alamein in early October and was attended by key African policymakers, original-equipment manufacturers (OEMs), investors, financiers and industrialists.
The agreement, which follows initial meetings facilitated by the African Association of Automotive Manufacturers, proposes to combine Malben Engineering’s established automotive manufacturing expertise with Elaraby Group’s extensive domestic industrial capability.
Established in Nigel in 1974, Malben Engineering has more than five decades of experience in supplying stampings and complex welded assemblies to leading OEMs operating in South Africa, including Ford Motor Company, BMW, Fiat, Alfa Romeo and Volkswagen.
The highly diversified Elaraby Group, meanwhile, operates through 16 companies spanning commercial, industrial, medical and service activities and employs more than 36 000 people in Egypt and the Middle East.
“Partnering with an established Egyptian industrial group could materially shorten Malben’s route to market and provide access to existing manufacturing capacity, people, administrative systems, procurement capability and local supplier relationships, avoiding many of the challenges associated with a greenfield startup,” Malben Engineering operational director Luca Smargiasso explains.
The Elaraby Group will contribute its established Egyptian industrial footprint, local operating capability, market knowledge and relationships.
The fact that both companies are family-owned businesses has also been cited as a factor in facilitating the relationship, with the Elaraby Group involving third-generation family members and Malben Engineering remaining a second-generation family enterprise, 52 years after its founding.
“As the partnership develops, the parties intend to explore joint investment opportunities in new facilities and capabilities serving Egypt's automotive industry, with the potential to support wider regional supply opportunities,” Smargiasso explains.
Technical director Marco Smargiasso adds that the proposed partnership is also aligned with Egypt’s National Automotive Industry Development Programme, which is designed to localise and deepen automotive manufacturing and develop the supporting components industry.
The framework links incentives to measurable outcomes, including local content, production volumes, investment and exports, and has some parallels with South Africa’s Automotive Production Development Programme.
There is also a longer-term opportunity to develop competitive African automotive supply chains through which components and manufacturing capability can increasingly be sourced within the continent rather than imported from outside Africa.
“As that capability develops, the African Continental Free Trade Agreement creates the potential to serve OEMs and automotive markets across the continent, subject to the applicable rules of origin and market-access requirements,” Smargiasso adds.
However, commercial director Marius Schafer says the immediate priority is to establish a competitive and sustainable operation in Egypt.

articles.title: ‘Nigeria’s Export Growth Lacks Industrial Value Addition’ - Independent Newspaper Nigeria
articles.summary: ‘Nigeria’s Export Growth Lacks Industrial Value Addition’  Independent Newspaper Nigeria
articles.full_text:
LAGOS – Nigeria’s rising export earnings are yet to translate into the level of industrial value addition required to transform the economy, as business leaders and economic experts called for urgent measures to lower production costs, deepen domestic value chains and make the country a competitive manufacturing and export hub in Africa.
The concern comes as the country seeks to leverage the Nigeria Industrial Policy 2025 to accelerate industrial development and reposition manufacturing as a stronger driver of investment, exports, productivity and employment.
President of the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria (MAN), Otunba Francis Meshioye, said the scale of the challenge was evident in Nigeria’s trade structure, noting that total exports rose to N85.13 trillion in 2025, while manufactured exports accounted for only N2.50 trillion, representing 2.94 percent of total exports.
He said despite the increase in overall export earnings, the share of manufactured exports had remained broadly unchanged over the past four years.
“This tells us something important: Nigeria is exporting more, but industrial value addition is not expanding at the pace required to transform the economy,” Meshioye said.
According to him, if Nigeria is to become Africa’s industrial hub, it must move beyond dependence on primary commodity exports and build productive capacity that enables Nigerian firms to compete across Africa and the global market.
The former Director-General of the National Chamber of Commerce, Industry, Mines and Agriculture (NACCIMA) and international trade expert, Dr. John Isemede, similarly blamed Nigeria’s lack of global competitiveness on unstable policies and inadequate private-sector participation in major trade and industrial decisions.
Isemede said government often took major trade and industrial decisions without adequately involving manufacturers and the organised private sector, resulting in policy somersaults that undermined business planning and investment.
He also faulted what he described as government’s fixation on imports, noting that while the Nigeria Customs Service was given revenue targets from import duties, there were no corresponding targets for production or exports across government agencies.
According to him, the financing environment remained hostile to Nigerian businesses, with local loans costing between 25 and 35 percent compared with 0-3 percent available to Chinese competitors.
He questioned the roles of the Bank of Industry (BOI) and the Nigerian Export-Import Bank (NEXIM), arguing that the institutions were established to promote industry and exports rather than focus primarily on declaring profits.
Isemede also lamented that Nigeria lacked an institution dedicated to training export managers despite having signed more than 700 trade agreements, while inadequate infrastructure and logistics continued to undermine the movement of goods.
He said the absence of a national carrier and shipping line, functional rail system, warehouses and dry ports had made it cheaper in some cases to import goods from Australia than move products from Lagos to Ghana, while intra-ECOWAS trade had remained at five percent after 51 years.
He further noted that Nigeria, despite being the world’s largest producer of yam, cassava and shea nuts, continued to export raw commodities because the abolition of commodity boards contributed to the collapse of value addition.
Isemede said cocoa was taken out of Nigeria cheaply and returned as chocolate at about 500 times the price, highlighting the economic losses associated with exporting raw materials rather than processed products.
He cited multiple taxation, border closures, inadequate commercial officers in Nigerian embassies and weak trade information as additional constraints, contrasting Nigeria with India and China, which he said had developed stronger export networks.
He called for a national export policy with clear targets, reservation of certain sectors for local businesses as practised in Ghana and South Africa, development of industrial clusters and stronger commercial diplomacy to connect Nigerian producers with international markets.
The Executive Director of the Centre for the Promotion of Private Enterprise (CPPE), Dr. Muda Yusuf, also said Nigeria had diversified what it produces more than what it exports, stressing that the country’s economic transformation remained incomplete.
He noted that while agriculture was once the dominant source of livelihoods and exports and petroleum subsequently reshaped public finance, sectors including telecommunications, banking, trade, construction, entertainment and digital services had expanded opportunities for Nigerian businesses and young people.
However, it said many farms still generated low yields, manufacturers operated with costly power and logistics, while too much employment remained concentrated in activities with low returns.
The Lagos Chamber of Commerce and Industry (LCCI) similarly said the next phase of Nigeria’s economic development must focus on reducing the cost of doing business, expanding productive capacity and creating an environment where businesses can invest, produce, employ, compete and expand with greater confidence.
Its President, Engr. Leye Kupoluyi, said Nigeria must move beyond economic stabilisation towards shared prosperity, with the ultimate test of reforms being whether businesses could produce more at lower cost and households could afford more with their incomes.
The stakeholders identified high production costs as one of the most significant barriers to competitiveness.
Meshioye listed inadequate and expensive power, high production input and logistics costs, weak protection against unfair trade practices, policy and regulatory uncertainty, inadequate infrastructure, and skills, technology and innovation gaps among the structural constraints confronting manufacturers.
He said the challenges were compounded by the cumulative cost of taxes and regulatory compliance, limited access to long-term industrial finance, weak domestic value chains and dependence on imported inputs.
LCCI also said the cost structure facing manufacturers, farmers, logistics operators, retailers and millions of small businesses remained elevated by energy and transportation costs, multiple taxation, infrastructure gaps, financing costs, regulatory charges, insecurity and logistics inefficiencies.
It described manufacturing as the “heart of economic prosperity”, saying Nigeria could not sustainably achieve mass employment and broad-based prosperity without a strong manufacturing and industrial base.
The chamber called for reliable and affordable energy, accelerated gas-to-industry projects, affordable long-term financing, infrastructure in industrial clusters, improved working capital for SMEs, lower regulatory costs and stronger domestic supply chains.
He said Nigeria needed to produce more domestically, employ more Nigerians and reduce dependence on imported goods.
CPPE, meanwhile, urged government to prioritise power supply, security in farming and commercial corridors, ports and logistics, agricultural yields, industrial competitiveness and enterprise-relevant skills.
Yusuf said public support for industry should be tied to investment, efficiency and export performance, with the objective of lowering the cost of producing in Nigeria and expanding the supply of goods and services citizens could afford.
On financing, MAN proposed the establishment of a Nigeria First Industrial Fund to provide long-term concessionary financing, support technology upgrading and promote local value addition.
LCCI similarly called for longer-tenor financing at rates compatible with productive investment, saying monetary stability must ultimately translate into improved credit conditions for businesses.
MAN also urged stronger foreign exchange support for productive manufacturers, alongside backward integration and greater use of locally available raw materials.
LCCI called for domestic production of industrial inputs, packaging materials, machinery, chemicals, agricultural inputs and other intermediate goods required by manufacturers.
On trade, MAN called for stronger trade-defence mechanisms against dumping, substandard imports and other unfair practices, while supporting Nigerian manufacturers to compete under the African Continental Free Trade Area.
LCCI said Nigeria must move beyond primary commodities towards value-added exports, arguing that becoming a major production and export hub would require investment in standards, certification, trade logistics, industrial clusters, trade finance, export infrastructure and market access.
The stakeholders further stressed the importance of policy consistency and regulatory predictability.
MAN urged consistency in fiscal, monetary, trade and industrial policies, while LCCI said frequent changes in taxes, levies, tariffs, regulations and administrative procedures increase uncertainty and discourage long-term investment.

articles.title: Mobile Money Fintech Ltd CEO calls for greater financial inclusion and stronger fraud protection in Ghana’s fintech sector - Tech Review Africa
articles.summary: Mobile Money Fintech Ltd CEO calls for greater financial inclusion and stronger fraud protection in Ghana’s fintech sector  Tech Review Africa
articles.full_text:
Date: 2026-10-12
By: Nana Appiah
Acquaye
The Chief Executive Officer of Mobile Money Fintech Limited, Haruna Shaibu, has called for greater financial inclusion, stronger fraud protection and deeper collaboration across Ghana's financial Technology ecosystem, highlighting the need to extend digital financial services to underserved communities and micro-enterprises.
Speaking at the Fintech
Media Development Series in Accra, held under the theme “Understanding Fintech,
Building Trust, Telling the Real Story”, Shaibu said the industry must focus
not only on business growth but also on improving financial health, protecting
customers and expanding opportunities for small businesses.
“Our mission remains very,
very simple, but very entrenched in the Ghanaian financial ecosystem,” he said,
noting that mobile money had evolved from a peripheral player into an important
part of Ghana’s financial system.
Shaibu said
micro-enterprises remained significantly excluded despite progress in expanding
digital financial services. He called for greater efforts to bring small
traders and entrepreneurs into the formal financial ecosystem, enabling them to
grow their businesses, create employment and contribute to Ghana’s economic
development.
He also highlighted
opportunities to deepen mobile money usage, noting that global adoption figures
showed a significant gap between registered accounts and active users. Citing
GSMA reports, he said approximately 2.3 billion mobile money accounts existed
globally, but only about 600 million were active, indicating room to increase
the frequency and range of digital transactions.
Shaibu identified digital
lending as an area of growing opportunity, particularly for individuals and
micro-businesses that struggle to access financing. Digital transaction
records, he said, can help providers assess customer behaviour and develop
credit-scoring models that support access to loans. He added that the vast
majority of the company’s customers repay their loans, while stressing the
importance of addressing abuse of the system responsibly.
He also called for
innovation in digital insurance, arguing that simply making traditional
insurance products available through mobile money platforms was not enough to
drive adoption. Instead, he said, providers should explore embedding insurance
into customers’ everyday transactions to make coverage more accessible.
Fraud and cybersecurity were
among the major challenges he highlighted. Shaibu recounted an attempted online
scam involving a fake pizza order that sought to obtain his personal
information and take over his WhatsApp account. Although device binding on his
mobile money account provided an additional safeguard, he said the incident
demonstrated how fraudsters exploit vulnerabilities across different digital
platforms.
“The responsibility on all
of us is to keep educating our customers and also build the necessary tools
that will help us address some of these things in our ecosystem,” he said.
Shaibu said addressing fraud
required coordinated action across financial services, telecommunications and
other digital platforms, as attacks increasingly move between systems. He
identified artificial intelligence as a potential tool for detecting and managing
fraud in real time, provided organisations can collaborate and share relevant
information.
Looking ahead, he identified
several developments likely to shape the fintech industry, including artificial
intelligence for fraud prevention, open finance, embedded financial services,
digital assets and cross-border interoperability.
He said embedded finance
could help customers access savings, investment and insurance products through
routine transactions, reducing the barriers associated with purchasing such
services separately. He also highlighted the potential of tokenised assets to
allow people to invest in smaller fractions of assets such as gold, making
investment opportunities more accessible.
On cross-border payments,
Shaibu said reducing regulatory and operational friction could unlock
opportunities for African businesses, particularly micro-enterprises seeking to
benefit from regional trade and the African Continental Free Trade Area.
He cited Ghana’s mobile
money ecosystem as an important example of digital financial infrastructure,
reporting that the industry processed GH¢3.37 trillion in transactions as of
August 2026. However, he cautioned that the figure represented total transactions
across the ecosystem, including agent-to-agent transfers, merchant payments and
consumer transactions, rather than money held in customer accounts.
He also said Mobile Money
Fintech Limited processed more than 26 million transactions daily, making
operational resilience, platform reliability and consumer protection essential.
The company invested in a major platform upgrade in the previous year to expand
capacity and support continued growth in Ghana’s fintech sector.
Shaibu said the company was
committed to working with other fintech firms, dedicated electronic money
issuers, industry associations and regulators to strengthen the ecosystem. He
pointed to stakeholder engagements, the Bank of Ghana-led 3i Summit and the
company’s group fintech summit as platforms for collaboration, innovation and
expanding opportunities for Ghanaian businesses across African markets.
“Trust is the centerpiece of
what we do,” he said, describing fraud prevention and cybersecurity as areas in
which investment could not be compromised.
He called for collective
efforts to build a secure, inclusive and sustainable financial ecosystem that
supports customers, strengthens businesses and creates lasting economic
opportunities for Ghanaians.

articles.summary: Stocks rise as oil prices tumble after Trump hails 'energy ceasefire'  eNCAZelensky says strikes on Ukraine infrastructure 'Putin's answer' to Trump on energy ceasefire  BBCKyiv says Russia hits energy targets despite Trump ceasefire announcement  Daily MaverickZelenskyy vows to retaliate if Russian strikes on Ukraine’s power grid continue  The GuardianUkraine accuses Russia of violating Trump’s energy ceasefire as EU imposes new sanctions  Times...
articles.full_text:
HONG KONG - Most stock markets rose on Monday as oil prices tumbled after Donald Trump announced an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine, which offset a fresh wave of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
Both main crude contracts sank more than one percent following the US president's declaration, even as it sparked astonishment in Kyiv, which also said Moscow had struck multiple power plants in the country.
"Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said early Sunday on Truth Social. "Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!"
His post came after he called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to halt attacks on Russian refineries and said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president" who would finally settle the war.
Zelensky appeared to express surprise at the announcement, saying he was seeking further details, but added that "Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well".
Russia has yet to confirm its agreement.
While the announcement was welcomed by Ukraine's allies, Trump had come under fire after declaring a temporary easing of US sanctions on Russian diesel, which European leaders and Kyiv said would only embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The drop in oil prices reversed an initial spike that came in response to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia at the weekend.
At least a dozen people were killed at Riyadh's international airport Saturday -- the deadliest attack on Saudi soil for more than a decade -- and another one died following a second strike on Sunday.
The assaults marked a sharp escalation in the Yemen war, where Riyadh has long militarily supported the internationally recognised government against the Houthis.
The Iran-backed group on Sunday claimed multiple attacks over the past 24 hours and threatened to keep targeting the kingdom's transit hubs, calling them "a theatre of operations for our forces".
"The market is no longer paying full geopolitical premium on every headline, and that is probably the most useful signal in the morning price action," wrote SPI Asset Management's Stephen Innes.
"A strike matters if it threatens real barrels, shipping lanes, refining capacity or insurance costs; otherwise, the market is getting increasingly reluctant to pay up simply because the geopolitical ticker flashes red.
"The physical market remains tight enough to keep Brent above $100, but futures are refusing to treat every new escalation as the start of another straight-line inflation shock."
The drop in oil prices provided support to most Asian markets, with Hong Kong, Sydney, Singapore, Wellington and Manila all up.
But Seoul and Taipei were dragged by losses in chipmakers SK hynix, Samsung and TSMC. Tokyo was closed for a holiday.
US futures were sharply higher.
- AFP

articles.title: The Turbulent Story of Greeks in South Africa - GreekReporter.com
articles.summary: The Turbulent Story of Greeks in South Africa  GreekReporter.com
articles.full_text:
Despite being persecuted and discriminated against for decades, Greeks in South Africa managed to rise socially and prosper, with several of them becoming quite successful and wealthy. Today, they remain one of the most important beacons of Hellenism among the diaspora.
A recent book by Greek scholar Antonis Chaldeos, entitled The Greek Community in South Africa, sheds light on the fascinating and turbulent history of the Greeks who first arrived and settled in Cape Town in the 1860s.
Chaldeos, who holds a PhD in History from the University of Johannesburg, is among the few Greek scholars conducting research and writing about the history of Greeks on the whole of the African continent. His impressive list of books include the history of the Greeks in Sudan, Tunisia, Mozambique, Burundi, Morocco, Ethiopia, and Egypt.
“Conducting research in Africa is difficult,” he tells Greek Reporter. “Access to registries and historical data is problematic, and of course, it’s very costly to travel for research. Also, Greek communities on the continent are widely spread in many African nations.”
In South Africa, he says, the first Greek migrants were seamen who arrived to the port of Cape Town around 1860, while thirty years later migrations increased, with most coming from Ithaca and Cephalonia and, to a lesser extent, from Aegean islands, such as Lemnos, Lesvos, and Samos.
At the end of the 19th century, the Greek community numbered 200 to 300 people. Those living in the Cape Town area were traders, while those living in the north of present-day South Africa in the then independent Transvaal Republic were miners.
“Miners had a very tough life. Many died of lung diseases,” Chaldeos explains.
Civil strife and racism in South Africa
In 1899, the second war between the Boers (Europeans of Dutch and French descent) and the British broke out. Greeks actually fought on both sides. There was a Greek legion of thirty to forty people that fought on the side of the British. The majority of Greeks, however, sided with the Boers, who fought to defend their territory from British colonists.
The first organized community of Greeks was called the Greek Community of Cape Town, which pre-existed as a Mutual Aid Association (1898) and was established as a community in 1902.
It was followed by similar groups in the communities of Pretoria, Johannesburg (1908), and Durban (1918). Gradually, and until the 1950s and 1960s, more and more Greek communities were established in more than twenty cities, with the Greek presence constantly growing.
“Greeks faced racism on an unprecedented scale in the period between 1915 to 1917,” Chaldeos tells Greek Reporter. He refers to the violent riots that broke out against Greek shops and businesses during this period.
“The riots were instigated by both the British and the Boers,” he explains. “This was because Greece remained neutral during the beginning of the First World War. They considered anyone who was not allied to their war effort to be their enemy.”
The violence was engineered “even though many Greek immigrants voluntarily left South Africa to join the forces of the Allied Powers,” Chaldeos notes.
Greeks integrated and became successful
Greeks—together with the Italians and the Spanish—were considered second-class citizens for decades, the Greek scholar says.
To counter discrimination, they tried to integrate into the local culture and political and social life. “But, they paid a price in their efforts to be assimilated. Among the younger generations, many do not speak Greek,” he explains.
Chaldeos says that an important achievement of the Greeks was the establishment of the SAHETI private school, a beacon of Greek-language education in South Africa. It was founded in 1974—decades after the arrival of the first Greek migrants—thanks to donations of Greeks from all over South Africa.
Until the 1930s, Greeks were mostly in the business of owning and operating tea rooms, i.e. places that served coffee, tea, and food. In the beginning, they had canteens that were opened in the cities and mainly in Johannesburg, the city with the largest population. Later, they established tea rooms that grew over the years.
In the 1940s and 1950s, the small tea rooms and shops owned by Greeks developed into supermarkets with branches all across the country. Greeks were also pioneers in the production and standardization of tobacco products in South Africa, but they also established beverage and water bottling factories, ore processing factories, and shipping companies among other types of major businesses.
The greatest migration flow took place after 1950 and mainly after 1960. After the end of World War II in Greece, several thousand Greeks went to South Africa, which at that time was looking for Europeans. Greeks from African countries that were gaining their independence, such as Egypt, Sudan, and the Congo, migrated to South Africa.
Decline in numbers
Around 1970, the Greek community numbered 120,000 people, but it began declining after 1976 when native Africans attempted to regain political control over their country, which had long been ruled by whites.
The riots in Soweto in 1976 alarmed Greeks, who slowly began to leave the country. The greatest wave of fleeing the country began in 1990, when the country passed from the regime of apartheid and white domination to a democratic country. The rise of crime and economic hardship that followed forced almost half of the remaining Greek population to leave the country. From 70,000 in 1990, today the Greeks of South Africa number only about 35,000.
Chaldeos says that the Greek people as a rule, tried to stay away from politics; however, as he notes, one Greek man in particular became world-famous on the side of Nelson Mandela: George Bizos, who was Mandela’s lawyer and one of the three writers of South Africa’s Constitution.
His name is linked to the struggle against racism, xenophobia, and apartheid and the values of solidarity, human rights, and democracy.
Another Greek who became famous, perhaps for the wrong reasons, was Dimitri Tsafendas, who murdered one of the staunchest defenders of apartheid, South African Prime Minister Hendrik Verwoerd on September 6, 1966.
“Despite all the difficulties, Greeks in South Africa persevered and adapted to the new land,” Chaldeos notes. “Several of them are among the richest in South Africa with great fortunes in the field of either real estate—mostly with department stores—or as owners of chains of hundreds of restaurants.”

articles.title: Egypt records near $3 bln BoP surplus in FY25/26 as FDI, remittances rise - Economy - Business - Ahram Online
articles.summary: Egypt records near $3 bln BoP surplus in FY25/26 as FDI, remittances rise - Economy - Business  Ahram Online
articles.full_text:
Egypt recorded an overall balance of payments (BoP) surplus of $2.8 billion in FY2025/26, which ends at end of June 2026, reversing a deficit of $2.1 billion a year earlier, as stronger foreign investment and remittances helped offset a widening current account deficit, according to Central Bank of Egypt (CBE) data released on Monday.
The capital and financial account recorded net inflows of $23.2 billion, up from $10.2 billion in FY2024/25, supported by higher foreign direct investment (FDI) and portfolio investment.
Net FDI inflows rose to $18 billion from $12.2 billion, while portfolio investment in Egypt increased to $4.2 billion from $1.6 billion.
The current account deficit, however, widened to $22.5 billion from $15.4 billion, reflecting a larger merchandise trade deficit and higher investment income payments, the CBE said.
Non-oil FDI recorded net inflows of $17.8 billion, compared with $11.6 billion in the previous fiscal year.
Greenfield investments and capital increases by existing companies generated inflows of $8.8 billion, including $3.5 billion during October–December 2025 from the implementation of the Alam Al-Roum deal.
Reinvested earnings increased to $6.2 billion from $4.2 billion, while non-resident purchases of Egyptian real estate generated $2.8 billion in net inflows, up from $1.9 billion.
FDI in the oil and mineral resources sector recorded net inflows of $190.2 million, down from $598.3 million a year earlier, as higher investment inflows were largely offset by increased outflows related to foreign partners’ cost recovery for exploration, development and operations.
Egypt’s merchandise trade deficit expanded by 27.1 percent to $64.8 billion in FY2025/26, up from $51 billion a year earlier.
The non-oil trade deficit widened by 25.4 percent to $46.6 billion, as import payments rose by 16.9 percent to $83.9 billion, outpacing the 7.8 percent increase in non-oil export proceeds to $37.3 billion.
Intermediate goods accounted for 55.2 percent of the total increase in non-oil imports. Export growth was concentrated in fresh and processed vegetables, gold, ready-made garments, household electrical appliances, and fresh and dried fruit.
The oil trade deficit increased by 31.5 percent to $18.3 billion. Oil imports rose by 27.6 percent to $24.9 billion, driven mainly by higher natural gas and crude oil imports. Oil exports, meanwhile, grew by 18.1 percent to $6.6 billion.
The investment income deficit also widened by 33.8 percent to $21.2 billion, as payments increased by $5.2 billion to $23.9 billion, while receipts fell to $2.7 billion.
Remittances from Egyptians working abroad rose by 29.6 percent to $47.3 billion in FY2025/26, up from $36.5 billion a year earlier, helping contain the increase in the current account deficit.
Tourism revenues increased by 10.3 percent to $18.4 billion from $16.7 billion, while net services receipts rose by 10.5 percent to $16.7 billion.
Suez Canal transit receipts climbed by 21.6 percent to $4.4 billion, compared with $3.6 billion in FY2024/25. Net tonnage transiting the canal increased by 22.4 percent to 590.8 million tons, while the number of transiting vessels rose by 9.8 percent to 13,600.
The CBE said the recovery in tourism revenues and Suez Canal receipts helped curb the widening current account deficit.
Medium- and long-term loans and facilities recorded net disbursements of $1.9 billion, reversing net repayments of $3.5 billion in the previous fiscal year.
Total disbursements reached $9 billion, compared with $8.9 billion, while principal repayments fell to $7.1 billion from $12.4 billion.
The CBE’s preliminary figures showed that the overall BoP surplus reached $2.8 billion, compared with a deficit of $2.1 billion in FY2024/25. The change in the CBE’s reserve assets reflected an increase of $2.8 billion during the year, against a decline of $2.1 billion a year earlier.
Both Fitch Ratings and S&P Global affirmed Egypt’s credit rating at “B” and ‘B/B’, maintaining a stable outlook as policy measures, resilient foreign currency inflows, and economic reforms help the country weather the impact of the Middle East conflict.

Ethiopia has inaugurated its first gold refinery, with an initial investment of $50 million, in a move aimed at strengthening domestic mineral processing, increasing the added value of exports, and positioning the country as a regional gold-refining hub in East Africa.
Reuters reported on Monday, October 12, 2026, that the project was established through an investment partnership in which state-owned Ethiopian Investment Holdings holds the majority stake, according to Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.
The new refinery is located in the Bole Lemi Special Economic Zone and is designed to process domestically produced gold, as well as receive gold from neighboring countries and regional mining companies. This would allow refining, testing, and documentation to be carried out within Africa rather than sending the metal to facilities outside the continent.
Integrated Gold Refining and Manufacturing Services
The refinery will provide a range of services, including gold smelting, assaying, refining, casting, bullion minting, and the production of blanks used in minting operations. These capabilities are intended to establish an integrated infrastructure supporting the gold trade and the development of the precious metals value chain.
Through the project, Ethiopia aims to retain a larger share of gold's economic value domestically, rather than exporting the metal in its raw form, relying on foreign facilities for processing, and subsequently purchasing higher-value products.
Gold Exports Support Foreign Exchange Earnings
The refinery's inauguration comes as gold remains one of Ethiopia's most important sources of foreign currency. The country's gold exports reached $5.6 billion last year, according to government data cited by Reuters.
The Ethiopian government expects domestic refining capacity to improve export quality, increase the economic returns generated by mineral resources, create specialized jobs, and attract refining business from other regional markets.
The project also represents a step toward expanding Ethiopia's role in the African precious metals trade by providing processing and documentation services to regional producers, potentially reducing the need to transport gold outside the continent to complete these operations.
The refinery reflects Ethiopia's broader strategy to strengthen the domestic processing of natural resources and increase the contribution of productive industries to exports and foreign exchange earnings, rather than relying solely on raw material exports.

articles.title: Ghana and BRICS: Strategic optionality or an expensive signal? (Part 1) - Adomonline.com
articles.summary: Ghana and BRICS: Strategic optionality or an expensive signal? (Part 1)  Adomonline.com
articles.full_text:
On 6 October 2026, Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa announced that President Mahama’s Cabinet has decided Ghana will apply to join BRICS.
The announcement came during a visit by India’s External Affairs Minister, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar.
Nothing has been decided beyond this intention: admission needs the agreement of existing members, no application date has been given and officials have not said whether Ghana would accept the lighter “partner country” status first.
Five points frame the rest of this article:
Ghana already trades heavily with BRICS economies.
Four of them (the UAE, India, South Africa and China) took roughly 57% of Ghana’s 2025 export earnings, from Ghana Statistical Service data.
Membership would formalise an existing pattern more than redirect trade.
The most useful financial tools are reachable without full membership
The New Development Bank (NDB) admits members who are not in BRICS and cedi-yuan settlement is already being piloted by Stanbic Bank Ghana, a commercial bank.
The main risk is sequencing, not the bloc itself
AGOA access expires on 31 December 2026, a bespoke US trade deal is unfinished and Ghana is rebuilding its standing with international investors after a debt default.
BRICS is a divided club
Its members include Iran, Russia and the UAE, and recent summits papered over sharp disagreements.
A staged approach looks stronger than a leap
Partner status, NDB membership and payment corridors capture much of the upside while keeping full membership as an option.
1. What has actually been announced
Ablakwa told reporters the Cabinet had decided to put in a formal application and that Ghana had already asked India, the BRICS chair for 2026, for help with the process.
He framed the move as diversification, saying Ghana will not walk away from traditional partners but wants “new friends”.
He stressed that Ghana remains a member of the IMF and the World Bank and cited roughly US$700 million of support from Afreximbank during the 2023–24 crisis as evidence that non-Western institutions already matter to Ghana.
Jaishankar was warm but careful. He described India as sympathetic to Ghana’s aspirations and called the request a matter for collective consideration by the bloc.
Two Ghana–India memoranda (agriculture, and science and technology) were signed alongside the announcement, with further cooperation flagged in railways, pharmaceuticals, ICT and defence.
What is not yet known: the date of the formal application, the category of membership Ghana will seek, any response from other members and what the government’s cost-benefit analysis shows.
The Minority in Parliament, led by the ranking member of the Foreign Affairs Committee, Samuel Abu Jinapor, has demanded an urgent briefing.
2. What BRICS membership is, and is not
It is a consensus club with two tiers
BRICS now lists 11 members: Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, plus Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the UAE and Indonesia, with Saudi Arabia invited but not publicly confirmed.
A separate partner tier, created in 2024, includes Nigeria and Uganda from Africa, along with Belarus, Bolivia, Cuba, Kazakhstan, Malaysia, Thailand, Uzbekistan and Vietnam.
Partners join selected activities but do not take part in the most consequential decisions. Egypt, Ethiopia and South Africa are the only African full members, and West Africa has none, so Ghana would be the first.
It is not a common currency
The September 2026 New Delhi summit endorsed work on payment-system interoperability and local-currency settlement, and it did not revive the idea of a BRICS currency.
Even the strongest example of de-dollarisation, India–Russia trade, reached its high share of national-currency settlement through bilateral arrangements, not a bloc-wide mechanism.
It is not a harmonious alliance
BRICS foreign ministers failed to agree a joint statement in May amid the war involving Iran, and the leaders’ declaration in September avoided condemning either the US-Israeli strikes or Iranian attacks on Gulf states.
Iran and the UAE are both members. This matters for Ghana because the UAE is its single largest export market.
It does include financial institutions
The NDB, headquartered in Shanghai, lends for infrastructure and sustainable development and has been asked by leaders to expand local-currency lending.
The Contingent Reserve Arrangement (CRA), a roughly US$100 billion liquidity backstop for members facing balance-of-payments stress, only serves members.
The September summit approved amendments to the CRA treaty and a further test run.
3. Why is Ghana moving now?
Several currents converge in late 2026.
A stabilised economy gives the government confidence.
The IMF Executive Board completed the sixth and final review of Ghana’s roughly US$3 billion Extended Credit Facility in July 2026 and moved Ghana to a 36-month Policy Coordination Instrument, which carries IMF monitoring but no new money.
The Fund says inflation fell sharply, reserves nearly doubled by 2025, the primary balance swung to surplus and the risk of debt distress returned to moderate.
Fitch upgraded Ghana to B (positive outlook) in May, Moody’s moved its outlook to positive on Caa1 in April, and S&P rates Ghana B-.
Western support is more transactional.
USAID has been dismantled and the United States proposed a health compact worth US$109 million over five years as a replacement.
Ghana’s Cabinet rejected it over health-data and specimen-sharing demands, with President Mahama calling the terms humiliating.
For context, US assistance to Ghana was about US$219 million in 2024, of which US$96 million was for health.
US tariffs on Ghanaian goods reached 15% in August 2025 before the Supreme Court ruled in February 2026 that the emergency-powers statute used to impose them does not authorise tariffs.
Other doors have opened
China began zero-tariff treatment for Ghana and other African partners on 1 May 2026. The Bank of Ghana says banks are already piloting cedi payments for Chinese imports, with Stanbic Bank Ghana live and GCB preparing a similar service.
India, after Prime Minister Modi’s July 2025 visit, has become a major buyer of Ghanaian gold and President Mahama says Ghana’s exports to India rose from about US$3 billion to nearly US$7 billion.
(Some reports describe the US$7 billion as two-way trade, so the figure should be treated with care.)
The policy narrative is resource sovereignty
The government wants to stop exporting raw materials and capture more value from gold, cocoa and minerals, a theme that links to its 24-Hour Economy and export programmes. BRICS is presented as another route to capital, technology and markets for that agenda.
SOCIO-ECONOMIC IMPLICATIONS
Trade: formalising what already exists
Ghana’s export base is narrow and tilted toward BRICS economies. Gold bullion was about two-thirds of export earnings in the fourth quarter of 2025, and the top five destinations took 71.2% of 2025 export earnings:
| Destination | Share of 2025 exports | BRICS status | 
| UAE | 25.9% | Member | 
| India | 16.0% | Member | 
| Switzerland | 14.2% | Not a member | 
| South Africa | 10.3% | Member | 
| China | 4.9% | Member | 
Adding the four BRICS rows gives about 57%. Much of this reflects the mechanics of the gold trade, which flows through Dubai, Indian refiners and South African and Swiss hubs, more than any strategic choice.
On imports, China is Ghana’s largest supplier, at roughly 22–23% of imports in recent quarters according to the Ghana Statistical Service.
The implication is that BRICS membership would not suddenly open new markets. Its value lies in lowering frictions with partners Ghana already depends on, and in giving Ghana a stronger negotiating voice with them.
The corollary is a concentration risk: deeper integration with a handful of gold and import counterparties does little for diversification.
Industrialisation and value addition
The government’s strongest argument is that Ghana wants to move up the value chain. Indian interest in pharmaceuticals and vaccine manufacturing, railways and agriculture fits that goal and the new India MoUs point in the same direction.
The evidence so far also carries a warning. China’s proposed purchase of Atlantic Lithium (about US$210 million), the developer of Ghana’s first lithium mine at Ewoyaa, would place the country’s first lithium output in a Chinese supply chain.
South-South partnership does not guarantee local processing. Whether Ghana gets value addition depends on contract terms, local-content rules and bargaining power, and BRICS membership does not set those.
Jobs and exposure to the West
The immediate employment risk is not BRICS but AGOA. The US duty-free preference programme runs for Ghana until 31 December 2026 and renewal is undecided.
Garments and cocoa products are the main beneficiaries, and the trade minister has said a single garment factory can employ up to 5,000 people.
The EU, meanwhile, is a long-standing cocoa market and its deforestation regulation takes effect on 30 December 2026.
Both are reminders that the livelihoods most exposed to Western rules are concentrated in sectors where Ghana has few substitutes.
Aid, health and sovereignty
The health compact episode shows where the public case for BRICS is strongest: a government that wants to negotiate without conditions it regards as intrusive.
But rejecting US$109 million over five years also has a cost, and Ghana has not yet shown how health financing will be replaced.
The Accra Reset initiative and Mahama’s health-sovereignty agenda are, so far, aspirations rather than funded programmes.
Distribution
Cheaper Chinese imports help consumers and importers but compete with local manufacturers.
Zero-tariff access to China helps cocoa and other exporters, but Ghana’s goods trade with China remains lopsided: Chinese figures put two-way trade at US$14.1 billion in 2025 with Ghana’s exports to China at US$2.67 billion, implying an imbalance of roughly US$1

articles.full_text:
A project to link Iraq’s oil fields to Syria’s Mediterranean coast is moving forward amid efforts to redraw oil export routes in the Middle East, at an estimated cost of at least $15 billion. It is driven by Baghdad’s need to reduce its reliance on the Strait of Hormuz, Damascus’s desire to restore its role in regional energy trade, and US interest in expanding infrastructure investment in both countries.
But the project has raised questions about conflicts of interest following revelations of commercial and financial ties between Thomas Barrack, the US ambassador to Türkiye and special presidential envoy for Iraq and Syria, and Ziad Ghandour, a businessman who founded the US firm TI Capital.
A Reuters investigation published on 9 October 2026 highlighted the relationship and the legal questions it raises. The US State Department said Barrack was complying with ethics rules and denied that he had any financial interest in the pipeline.
The investors include a consortium led by a Qatari company and involving two US firms, while talks are under way for a major French group to join. Studies into the project’s financing, ownership and operation continue amid financial, security and technical challenges that could mean it takes years to implement.
From Barrack to Ghandour: A network of interests behind the oil project
The Reuters investigation found that Thomas Barrack encouraged TI Capital, founded by Ziad Ghandour, to become involved in a project to transport Iraqi oil to Syria’s Baniyas port. It cited three people familiar with efforts concerning the project, including two sources with direct knowledge of discussions with Iraqi and Syrian officials.
Barrack, an American businessman who founded the investment firm Colony Capital, has business ties with Ghandour dating back years before he took up his diplomatic post.
Documents filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission in March 2021 showed that the two men co-founded Falcon Acquisition, which sought to raise $250 million through an initial public offering. Barrack chaired its board, while Ghandour was its chief executive.
The company’s plans faltered after Barrack was arrested in July 2021 on charges related to acting on behalf of the UAE without registering under US law. A US jury acquitted him in November 2022. The acquisition company partnership ended, but Barrack retained other financial interests in a project managed by Ghandour’s company.
In a financial disclosure filed with the US Office of Government Ethics in March 2025, Barrack acknowledged retaining an interest in ACD-TI Oakley Investment, which is linked to a real estate project in Oakley, California, and managed by Ghandour’s company. Under the arrangement, he is entitled to receive 20 per cent of profits above a 15 per cent return threshold in exchange for services he previously provided to the company. He also disclosed that he provided it with advisory services during 2024.
In an ethics agreement signed on 7 March 2025, Barrack pledged to refrain from personal and substantial participation in government matters that directly and predictably affect his financial interests, unless he receives a legal waiver or a regulatory exception applies.
Ghandour has been arranging energy investments for more than two decades. US documents from 2003 and 2004 showed that his company contracted with the US energy firm Centroleum to help arrange negotiations with international companies, including Saudi Aramco and Spain’s Repsol. The agreements included financial arrangements tied to shares and financing.
Efforts concerning the Iraq-Syria oil project date back to May 2026, when Barrack floated the idea of involving Ghandour’s company during a meeting on the sidelines of the Milken Global Conference in Los Angeles. The two men also took part in a closed session on the need to develop new routes for energy supplies in the Middle East.
On 16 June, TI Capital was named in a statement issued by Barrack and Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi. They praised progress towards signing a memorandum of understanding with the company to revive the Kirkuk-Baniyas pipeline. An announcement in July then unveiled a broader consortium that included US-based Chevron and Qatar’s UCC.
These developments show how the relationship between Barrack and Ghandour evolved from an investment partnership and financial interests to the diplomatic efforts that preceded Ghandour’s company joining the pipeline project.
Reuters quoted a person close to Barrack as saying the US envoy trusts Ghandour’s ability to help implement the strategy of President Donald Trump’s administration to draw Iraq and Syria closer to the US.
These efforts have raised questions among government ethics experts. Richard Painter, the former chief White House ethics lawyer and a law professor at the University of Minnesota, said Barrack’s relationship with Ghandour poses a serious problem under federal rules governing the impartiality of government employees. He argued that the US envoy should recuse himself entirely from discussions of the project.
Don Fox, former general counsel and acting director of the US Office of Government Ethics, also said that a government official promoting a company with which he has a business relationship could violate rules barring the use of public office to endorse private entities.
US federal ethics rules govern officials’ participation in matters involving people or companies with whom they have business or personal relationships that could cast doubt on their impartiality. The rules also allow the relevant government authority to assess such cases and grant permission to participate.
A records request filed by Reuters showed that the US Office of Government Ethics had no waiver on record concerning Barrack’s participation in the project in light of his relationship with Ghandour’s company. The State Department, however, said Barrack has no stake, role or financial interest in the Kirkuk-Baniyas pipeline. It said his actions are consistent with US policy encouraging regional integration in the energy sector and stressed his compliance with ethics rules.
Ghandour’s company also appeared in a consortium studying the development of the Akkas gas field in Anbar province, alongside UCC and the US oil company ConocoPhillips, according to the Reuters investigation. TI Capital’s website also lists its involvement in projects linked to Syria’s Tartus port.
The consortium and financing: Who will own and operate the pipeline?
On 4 July 2026, the Iraqi cabinet approved authorising the state-owned Basra Oil Co. to sign a preliminary agreement on principles and a non-disclosure agreement with a consortium including TI Capital, Chevron and UCC. The agreements cover technical and financial studies for two proposed oil export routes: one to Türkiye’s Ceyhan port and the other to Syria’s Baniyas port, through a network starting in Basra and passing through Anbar province.
The Iraqi government’s decision said the agreements concern preparing studies and assessing routes, while negotiations continue over the final financial and contractual commitments. The cabinet also approved completing an advisory contract with the US engineering services company KBR for the Basra-Haditha line inside Iraq.
On 17 July, the Iraqi and Syrian governments signed a memorandum of understanding to develop the oil corridor at a ceremony hosted by the US Chamber of Commerce in Washington. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi attended, alongside officials from both countries and representatives of the participating companies.
The signing took place during a visit in which more than 50 agreements, memorandums of understanding and partnerships were announced, worth more than $60 billion in total, according to a US Chamber of Commerce statement issued on 18 July.
The following day, the investor consortium announced that it had signed separate agreements on principles with the two governments through three business entities: Qatar’s UCC OrbaCon for Investment in Concessions, Chevron Business Development for Europe, the Middle East and Africa, and Tech Infra 2, affiliated with the TI Capital Group.
According to the statement, UCC is coordinating the consortium, while the companies prepare technical and financial feasibility studies and an initial financing plan. A joint Iraqi-Syrian working group is also being formed to address cross-border issues. Ownership stakes, operating rights, transit fees and concession periods remain subject to the completion of negotiations and government approvals.
A prominent member of the consortium is Qatar’s UCC Holding, part of Power International Holding. Its chairman is Qatari businessman Moataz Al Khayyat, while his brother Ramez serves as chief executive.
The company has expanded its investments in Syria. In May 2025, the Syrian government signed a memorandum of understanding with a UCC-led consortium to develop power generation projects, with announced investments of about $7 billion. Thomas Barrack attended the signing ceremony in Damascus.
In November that year, final concession agreements were signed with a consortium led by the company to develop, expand and operate Damascus International Airport. The announced investments totalled about $4 billion and involved Turkish and American companies, as part of UCC’s expansion into Syrian infrastructure projects.
Chevron, one of the largest US oil and gas companies, is participating in the corridor’s preliminary studies as part of its broader interest in Iraq’s oil sector, including negotiations over the development of the West Qurna 2 and Nasiriyah fields.
The list of potential investors expanded when French energy company TotalEnergies entered talks on the project. What multi-million-dollar Dar Port expansion means for investors, TZ
DAR ES SALAAM: THE transformation of Dar es Salaam Port from a congested bottleneck into East and Central Africa’s most competitive trade artery is entering a decisive phase through a multibillion-dollar infrastructure push aimed at delivering tangible benefits for citizens, businesses and investors alike.
What began as a World Bank-financed project in 2017, with a 345 million US dollars (about 919.9bn/-) credit through the International Development Association, has evolved into a comprehensive modernisation programme that is reshaping regional trade dynamics and positioning Tanzania as the gateway of choice for seven landlocked nations.
Speaking during the ground-breaking ceremony for 701.8bn/- oil storage tanks at the port on March 3, 2026, President Dr Samia Suluhu Hassan said ongoing port reforms had enhanced operational efficiency, expanded cargo-handling capacity and strengthened government revenue performance.
She added that the project forms part of the government’s broader strategy to strengthen transport infrastructure and enhance Tanzania’s competitive position as a regional trade hub.
A port reborn: From 12 berths to 22
The physical transformation is the most visible evidence of this strategic push. Chief Government Spokesperson and permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Information, Culture, Arts and Sports Mr Gerson Msigwa confirmed that the expansion involves the construction of ten new berths, increasing the total from 12 to 22, at a cost of approximately 2 billion US dollars (about 5tri/- ).
The port deepening programme, in two phases, has seen the entrance channel deepened from 10 metres to 15.5 metres, enabling the facility to accommodate large vessels of up to 8,000 containers, compared with about 4,000 previously, while bulk carriers can carry up to 70,000 tonnes.
Minister for Transport Professor Makame Mbarawa confirmed during an inspection tour that the second phase, costing 219bn/-, would allow the port to receive larger ships and reduce shipping costs.
Private sector partnerships delivering results
Central to the port’s revival has been the strategic engagement of private operators. The Tanzania Ports Authority (TPA) signed concession agreements with DP World and Adani International Ports, establishing DP World Dar es Salaam Limited and Tanzania East Africa Gateway Terminal Limited.
Mr Msigwa noted that as of June 2025, DP World had invested approximately 214.2bn/- in new equipment and modern systems. Tanzania East Africa Gateway Terminal Limited (TEAGTL) is investing 410.4bn/- in infrastructure rehabilitation and upgrades to Berths 8 to 11.
The impact has been dramatic. Ship turnaround times for container vessels have fallen from an average of 30 days to just six days. Cargo volumes rose to 27.7 million tonnes in 2024/2025, a 17 per cent increase.
According to Port Director Mr Abed Gallus, the facility handled a total cargo throughput of 33.71 million tonnes in the 2025/26 financial year, representing a 21.5 per cent increase from the previous year.
TPA Director General Plasduce Mbossa attributed these gains to sustained investment. “Port efficiency has increased by approximately 98 per cent due to the reduction in vessel service times. This is a sign that Tanzania has begun to reap the benefits of the substantial investments made in the port sector under the leadership of President Dr Samia Suluhu Hassan,” he said.
Benefits to citizens and businesses
For Tanzanian businesses and citizens, the port modernisation is delivering tangible dividends. The elimination of the 1,000 US dollars container demurrage fee has resulted in annual savings of 600 million US dollars (about 1.5tri/-) for traders.
The partnership with DP World has generated 325.3bn/- in government revenue through land rent, royalties and wharfage charges.
Perhaps most importantly, the expansion is creating jobs. Mr Msigwa confirmed that direct employment had reached 764 jobs as of June 2025, with thousands of indirect jobs created. Industry stakeholders report that over 30,000 direct jobs and 150,000 indirect jobs have been generated.
Tanzania Shipping Agents Association Chairman Daniel Malongo said the engagement of private operators had improved efficiency. “This has been a key driver behind the sustained growth in cargo volumes,” he said.
Tanzania Freight Forwarders Association Executive Secretary Liston Goodluck added, “As operational efficiency continues to improve, more cargo owners are choosing the Port of Dar es Salaam because it offers a faster and more reliable gateway to regional markets.”
ALSO READ: Dar Port climbs 105 places in the CPPI index from 360th to 255th position in 2025 rankings
Serving seven landlocked nations
The port’s strategic importance extends far beyond Tanzania’s borders. In the 2024/2025 financial year, Tanzanian ports handled approximately 12.6 million tonnes of transit cargo. The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) led with nearly 6 million tonnes, followed by Zambia with 3.5 million tonnes and Rwanda with 1.7 million tonnes.
In the 2025/2026, transit cargo rose 17 per cent to 14.61 million tonnes, driven heavily by regional markets: Transit to DRC rose by 30 per cent to 7.77 million tonnes (accounting for over half of transit traffic), Rwanda up 24 per cent to 2.18 million tonnes and Zambia: 3.41 million tonnes (slightly down 5 per cent).
According to Mr Gallus, rising cargo volumes are creating pressure on road infrastructure outside the port, with about 3,000 trucks handling cargo around the port each day.
To address the challenge, TPA is promoting greater use of rail, inland container depots and logistics centres. Facilities in Morogoro and Isaka will help distribute cargo closer to its final destinations, while the Standard Gauge Railway (SGR) is increasingly being used to move containers from Dar es Salaam.
The integration of SGR with port operations is central to this regional strategy. Prof Mbarawa confirmed that the 68,000-square-metre cargo terminal in Morogoro would have capacity to handle 600 containers per day. Dry ports are being developed in Kurasini Phase II, Kwala, Ihumwa and Chuo cha Polisi area.
A strategic asset in a changing world
According to the 2025 Container Port Performance Index published by the World Bank, Dar es Salaam climbed 105 places globally from 360th in 2024 to 255th in 2025, making it the highest-performing port in East Africa.
Mombasa fell from 375th to 396th. TPA Director of Marketing and Communications George Fasha said the Port Infrastructure Development Levy had been reduced from 9 per cent to 4.5 per cent of customs duty. “This adjustment demonstrates that TPA has listened to stakeholders,” he said.

articles.title: Ethiopia opens 600-tonne precious metals refinery as it targets Africa’s gold-processing business - Business Insider Africa
articles.summary: Ethiopia opens 600-tonne precious metals refinery as it targets Africa’s gold-processing business  Business Insider AfricaEthiopia launches its first gold refinery, Prime Minister says  Reuters
articles.full_text:
- Ethiopia has opened a refinery designed to process more than 600 tonnes of precious metals annually.
- The project brings together Ethiopian Investment Holdings and Dubai-based Sam Precious Metals.
- It will produce gold and silver bars while seeking customers across Africa.
- The capacity figure represents potential processing volume, rather than current production.
Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed inaugurated the National Precious Metals Refinery on 10 October at the Bole Lemi Special Economic Zone in Addis Ababa.
The facility was established through a partnership between Ethiopian Investment Holdings and Sam Precious Metals, a Dubai-headquartered company that also operates in Egypt.
It is designed to test precious metals, refine gold into export-ready bullion and manufacture cast and minted gold and silver bars. The stated annual capacity covers precious metals collectively, rather than gold alone.
According to the Ethiopian prime minister’s office, the refinery will support domestic processing, improve quality assurance and help establish Ethiopia as a regional centre for precious metals refining and manufacturing. The more-than-600-tonne figure applies at full capacity.
A bid for Africa’s gold business
The government says the facility can serve neighbouring countries and mining companies across Africa, providing refining, testing and certification before their metal reaches buyers.
That would give participating producers an African processing option instead of sending their gold outside the continent. Ethiopia could also earn income from refining other countries’ output.
Mining gold and preparing it for sale are separate stages of the business. Refining removes impurities, while testing establishes the precious metal content used to determine its value.
The new facility could support both bullion exports and jewellery manufacturing, two activities identified in the government’s announcement. However, the opening statements do not name regional customers or establish how much metal the refinery is currently handling.
An established refining partner
Sam Precious Metals already offers gold and silver refining, minting and testing services through its operations in Dubai and Cairo.
The company had previously identified the Ethiopian facility as part of its expansion into precious metals-producing countries. Its involvement gives the project a partner with an existing refining business and international commercial relationships.
For Ethiopia, the commercial challenge is now securing enough metal to use the plant’s capacity and persuading producers to bring their business to Addis Ababa.
The opening establishes the infrastructure for that ambition. Actual throughput, customer contracts and the facility’s international accreditation will determine how far it can expand Ethiopia’s role in Africa’s gold trade.

Addressing the situation, the Egyptian Armed Forces emphasized the enduring bond between both countries, stating that the peaceful presence of millions of Sudanese citizens in Egypt serves as "clear evidence of the longstanding relationship between the two nations".
Egyptian Military leaders also advised residents across the region to rely on official news channels and "avoid being influenced by misleading rumors or foreign agendas seeking to undermine the fraternal ties between the Egyptian and Sudanese peoples".

Egypt today reported that Foreign Ministry spokesperson Nader Zaki confirmed that both officials underscored "the importance of mutual respect for each country's sovereignty, territorial integrity, and borders".

11 Okt 2026 16:28 WIB · Politik & Hukum
JAKARTA, KOMPAS — Indonesia and Egypt have agreed to strengthen economic cooperation through the establishment of an Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA) and a Joint Investment Fund. Under this new framework, the two countries are targeting bilateral trade volume to reach US$5 billion, or nearly Rp 89.5 trillion, by 2030.
The agreement was reached during the state visit of Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi to Indonesia, which was directly received by President Prabowo Subianto at the Merdeka Palace, Jakarta, Sunday (11/10/2026).
El-Sisi arrived at the Merdeka Palace at around 10:30 AM and was welcomed with a state ceremony. The two then held a bilateral meeting and signed a memorandum of understanding for approximately 2.5 hours, which was followed by a joint press statement.
During the visit, President Prabowo was accompanied by several ministers from the Red and White Cabinet, including Coordinating Minister for Human Development and Culture Sugiono, Coordinating Minister for Downstream and Energy Transition Bahlil Lahadalia, Minister of Foreign Affairs Arrmanatha Nasir, and Minister of Defense Sjafrie Sjamsoeddin.
Also present were the Minister of Investment and Downstream Industry Rosan Roeslani, the Minister of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries Sakti Wahyu Trenggono, the Minister of Agriculture Andi Amran Sulaiman, the Minister of Religious Affairs Nasaruddin Umar, the Minister of State Secretary Prasetyo Hadi, and the Cabinet Secretary Teddy Indra Wijaya.
The Egyptian delegation present included the Head of the Presidential Secretariat Ahmed Mohamed Aly Mohamed Sayed Ahmed; the Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation, and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Ahmed Mohamed Abdelatty; as well as the Minister of Transportation Kamel AbdelHady Farag ElWazir. Furthermore, the Minister of Investment and Foreign Trade Mohamed Farid Mohamed Saleh, the Minister of Industry Khaled Hashem Ali Maher, and the Director of the Presidential Office Kenselir Omar Alskhattab Marwan Abdallah Arafa were also in attendance.
Prabowo stated that the two countries have agreed to strengthen cooperation in various sectors, particularly in the economic, trade, and investment sectors. To achieve this, the two countries have pushed for the establishment of an Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA) between Indonesia and Egypt. This agreement is expected to open broader opportunities for increased market access, investment flows, and active business involvement from both countries.
Furthermore, Prabowo also welcomed the initiative to establish a Joint Investment Fund. This initiative, initiated by investment institutions from both countries, aims to encourage investment in various strategic projects going forward.
"We have pushed for the establishment of an Economic Partnership Agreement between Indonesia and Egypt to open up broader opportunities for market access, investment, and business engagement between the two countries," Prabowo said during a joint press statement.
The idea of establishing an EPA marks a new chapter in the economic relationship between the two countries. Trade cooperation between Indonesia and Egypt has previously been conventional, without a comprehensive, high-level trade agreement such as an FTA or EPA. The relationship between the two countries has previously relied primarily on a general trade framework and regular evaluations through a Joint Trade Committee.
In addition to economic cooperation, the two countries agreed to strengthen their relationship in the political field through the optimization of bilateral mechanisms and regular high-level consultations. In the maritime and fisheries sector, Indonesia and Egypt are committed to building a sustainable partnership that includes the conservation of marine resources, the eradication of illegal fishing, and the exchange of knowledge and expertise.
In the field of defense, both leaders agreed to enhance collaboration in the defense industry, improve capacity through education and joint training, as well as facilitate exchange visits between leaders and experts.
On that occasion, Prabowo also expressed appreciation to Egypt for its assistance and facilitation of the needs of the Navy's TNI ships in the peacekeeping mission in the Middle East.
According to Prabowo, this close bilateral relationship is also supported by strong ties between the communities, particularly in the education sector. This is evident from the large number of Indonesian students studying in Egypt, complementing the historical cooperation with Al-Azhar University, which is now increasingly developing, one of which is through the provision of teaching Indonesian language and literature at the university.
In the future, Indonesia is ready to expand educational cooperation through student exchanges, partnerships between universities, joint research, and inviting educational institutions and educators from Egypt to come to the country. In addition, the Indonesian government also expressed appreciation and welcomed the additional scholarship offers from Egypt, particularly in the fields of medicine, engineering, and science.
This series of state visits was marked by the signing of several memorandums of understanding to strengthen the relationship between the two countries. The agreements include an action plan for strategic partnership between the foreign ministries of both countries, visa exemption for holders of diplomatic, service, and special passports, as well as cooperation in the fields of statistics and the marine-fisheries sector.
"These agreements demonstrate our shared commitment to continue strengthening the Indonesia-Egypt strategic partnership," Prabowo said.
Furthermore, both leaders sought to align their perceptions and strengthen coordination in addressing various global and regional strategic issues. During the meeting, President Prabowo and President El-Sisi expressed deep concern over the escalation of conflict in the Middle East, particularly the worsening humanitarian crisis in Palestine due to Israeli military operations and serious violations of international law.
Indonesia and Egypt agreed to strongly condemn various provocative actions, the construction of illegal settlements, and the casualties among unarmed civilians such as children, women, and the elderly. In facing this situation, President Prabowo emphasized that the two-state solution remains the key to resolving the conflict.
"In our view, Indonesia firmly believes that the establishment of a Palestinian state based on the two-state solution is the only way to achieve peace in the region," said Prabowo.
Both countries are fully committed to continuing to promote the peace process, providing emergency humanitarian assistance, and supporting the recovery and reconstruction process in Gaza. Amid the escalating global situation, Indonesia and Egypt urge for the de-escalation of the conflict, cessation of violence, and the resumption of dialogue and diplomacy based on the Charter of the United Nations to ensure the safety of civilians and global economic stability.
These agreements represent a shared commitment to continue strengthening the Indonesia-Egypt strategic partnership.
Meanwhile, President El-Sisi stated that the bilateral relationship between Egypt and Indonesia is built on rich historical and civilizational roots. Egypt is recorded as one of the first countries to recognize Indonesia's independence and establish diplomatic relations in 1947, followed by the historical closeness of both countries in defending the interests of developing nations through the Asia-Africa Conference in Bandung.
"And today, both countries continue to take steps as pioneers in supporting security and stability in their regional environment, while consistently maintaining coordination and consultation on various regional and international issues of mutual interest," said El-Sisi.
President El-Sisi emphasized the importance of translating historical closeness and strategic partnerships into concrete cooperation projects. This cooperation will subsequently be followed up directly by the relevant agencies from both countries.
As a follow-up, both leaders agreed on an initial framework to strengthen economic and trade cooperation that is commensurate with the significant potential of both countries. This commitment is manifested through an ambitious target to boost bilateral trade volume to exceed 5 billion US dollars by 2030, accompanied by ongoing efforts to reduce various trade barriers.
Based on trade data from the last three years, the economic trends of both countries show a consistently upward graph. The total bilateral trade between Indonesia and Egypt was recorded at around USD 1.6 billion in 2023, then increased to approximately USD 1.73 billion in 2024, and is projected to accelerate towards USD 2.4 billion by the end of 2025.
Key commodities such as crude palm oil (CPO), coffee, spices, and manufactured products continue to dominate the market in Egypt. Meanwhile, Egypt supplies the raw material needs for industry and fertilizers to Indonesia.

Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty called for expanding trade, investment and industrial cooperation with Thailand during talks with Thai Industry Minister Varawut Silpa-archa in Bangkok on Monday, October 12, 2026.
The meeting focused on strengthening economic relations between the two countries, encouraging joint manufacturing projects and attracting Thai investment to Egypt, particularly in the Suez Canal Economic Zone (SCZONE).
Abdelatty, who also serves as Minister of International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates, praised Thailand's industrial progress in innovation, digital transformation and sustainability.
He expressed Egypt's interest in drawing on Thai expertise to develop domestic manufacturing, increase local production and expand industrial exports.
Egypt and Thailand Discuss Joint Manufacturing Opportunities
During the meeting, Abdelatty called for greater exchanges of economic and trade delegations to explore investment opportunities and establish partnerships between Egyptian and Thai businesses.
He stressed the importance of improving access to both countries' markets and encouraging joint manufacturing in several priority industries, particularly rubber, petrochemicals and tyres, where Thailand has established industrial expertise.
The Egyptian minister also presented the investment opportunities available in the Suez Canal Economic Zone, citing its industrial facilities, ports, logistics infrastructure and strategic location near major international shipping routes.
He said Egypt's network of free trade agreements with several countries could provide Thai manufacturers with additional opportunities to reach markets in Africa, the Middle East and Europe.
Suez Canal Economic Zone Attracts Thai Investment
Abdelatty welcomed the investment by Thai company Hi-Tech Apparel, describing it as the first Thai industrial project in the Suez Canal Economic Zone.
The company is developing a $20 million sportswear manufacturing facility in the Qantara West industrial zone in Ismailia.
According to the SCZONE, the project covers approximately 64,000 square metres and is expected to create around 2,000 direct jobs.
Once fully operational, the facility is designed to produce approximately six million garments annually, primarily for export markets in Europe and the United States.
In March 2026, Hi-Tech Apparel reported progress on construction, with garment manufacturing facilities scheduled for completion in May and a fabric mill planned for later in the year.
Abdelatty said the investment could serve as a foundation for attracting additional Thai manufacturers to Egypt across other industrial sectors.
For his part, Silpa-archa welcomed the longstanding relations between Egypt and Thailand and expressed interest in expanding industrial, commercial and investment cooperation.
He described Egypt as a potential gateway to African, Arab and European markets and expressed Thailand's interest in exploring further manufacturing and investment opportunities within the Suez Canal Economic Zone.
The talks took place during Abdelatty's visit to Bangkok, the first by an Egyptian foreign minister in three decades, as both countries seek to develop closer economic and commercial relations.
