articles.title: IMF Warns Europe’s Growth Will Slow as Russia’s War, Middle East Crisis Drive Up Energy Costs - Kyiv Post
articles.summary: IMF Warns Europe’s Growth Will Slow as Russia’s War, Middle East Crisis Drive Up Energy Costs  Kyiv Post
articles.full_text:
Economic growth in the eurozone is expected to slow to just 1.1% in 2026 as Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine and escalating conflict in the Middle East push energy prices higher, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) warned in its latest World Economic Outlook.
The forecast, released Tuesday, Oct. 13, represents a modest 0.2-percentage-point upgrade from July but remains below the 1.2% growth recorded in 2025.
The IMF expects the eurozone economy to expand by only 1.2% in 2027, with persistently high energy costs, weak consumer confidence and inflation continuing to constrain economic activity.
The Fund forecasts eurozone inflation at 3.1% this year and 2.8% next year – both significantly above the European Central Bank’s 2% target.
The figures underscore Europe’s vulnerability to energy disruptions as Russia continues its invasion of Ukraine and instability across the Middle East threatens global oil and natural gas supplies.
Russia’s war and Middle East crisis expose Europe’s energy vulnerability
The IMF warned that elevated energy costs could continue weighing on European households and businesses through next year.
Europe remains particularly vulnerable because many of its economies depend heavily on imported oil and natural gas.
The Fund warned that gas storage levels in parts of Europe remain below normal seasonal levels, potentially exposing consumers to further price increases during the winter heating season.
The combination of higher energy costs and persistent inflation could force the European Central Bank to maintain restrictive interest rates, limiting household spending and business investment.
The IMF expects underlying inflation to return to the ECB’s 2% target only around mid-2028, suggesting that price pressures could persist even if economic growth remains weak.
The latest projections also follow a volatile period for the eurozone economy, which recorded no growth in the first quarter of 2026 before rebounding by 2.6% in the second quarter.
Germany outperforms France as UK faces slower growth
The IMF projects significant differences among Europe’s largest economies.
Germany, the EU’s biggest economy, is expected to grow by 1.3% in 2026, while Spain is forecast to maintain stronger expansion of 2.5%.
France faces a much weaker outlook, with growth projected at just 0.4%, compared with 0.9% in 2025.
French unemployment is expected to rise to 8.4%, up from 7.7% last year.
For Britain, the IMF raised its 2026 growth forecast to 1.3%, an increase of 0.3 percentage points from July.
However, UK growth is expected to slow to 1.2% in 2027 as higher energy prices and borrowing costs weigh on consumption and investment.
The diverging forecasts reflect the uneven economic consequences of energy shocks and financial pressures across Europe.
IMF warns Middle East oil exporters face sharp contraction
During the World Economic Outlook press briefing, IMF officials said the economic consequences of the Middle East conflict differ sharply between oil-producing and oil-importing countries.
An IMF official said the Fund had revised its forecasts shortly before publication to account for higher oil prices, while warning that further escalation could worsen the outlook.
“We actually revised in the last minute almost our forecast to incorporate the higher oil prices,” the official said.
For Gulf oil exporters, the IMF forecasts a sharp contraction in production and exports, followed by a strong rebound in 2027, assuming conditions develop as projected.
Some of these economies are also experiencing slower growth in non-oil sectors.
Oil-importing countries, however, received modest forecast upgrades in several cases, supported by domestic demand, remittances and tourism.
Egypt was among the countries benefiting from upward revisions for both 2026 and 2027, partly because of a recovery in Suez Canal activity and petroleum-related industries.
But officials warned that renewed Houthi attacks and disruptions around the Bab al-Mandab Strait could jeopardize regional trade, shipping and economic activity.
AI boom shields global trade – but raises new economic risks
The IMF also highlighted the growing importance of artificial intelligence in sustaining international trade despite geopolitical instability.
Responding to questions from Bloomberg and Reuters about whether the global economy could face a recession if the AI investment boom collapsed, an IMF official said demand for AI-related products had made a substantial contribution to trade growth.
Global trade expanded by a cumulative 8.3% between 2023 and 2025, while trade in AI-related goods increased by 29%.
Without AI-related products, overall trade growth would have reached just 4.6%, according to the Fund’s calculations.
The IMF outlined several possible scenarios for the technology boom.
In the most favorable case, continued investment in AI would generate genuine productivity improvements, strengthening economic activity without adding to inflation.
A less favorable scenario would see investment and demand remain strong without corresponding productivity gains, producing weaker growth benefits and greater inflationary pressure.
The Fund is also examining the consequences of investors reassessing expected profits from AI, potentially triggering a correction in asset prices.
The IMF’s latest assessment suggests that the technology sector has become an increasingly important source of global economic resilience, even as its future contribution remains uncertain.

Addis Ababa [Ethiopia], October 11 (ANI): External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar on Sunday said he discussed ways to deepen investment partnerships between India and Ethiopia during a meeting with Brook Taye, CEO of Ethiopian Investments Holdings, in Addis Ababa on Saturday (local time).
"Pleased to meet Brook Taye, CEO, Ethiopian Investments Holdings. Discussed deeper investments partnerships between India and Ethiopia," Jaishankar said in a post on X.
During his visit, Jaishankar also chaired a conference of India's Heads of Mission in Africa, where discussions focused on strengthening cooperation between India and African countries across trade, investment, connectivity, development partnership and capacity building.
"Chaired today in Addis Ababa a conference of our Heads of Mission in Africa. India and Africa share deep linkages built upon Global South solidarity, strategic autonomy, multipolarity and common development aspirations. We held in depth discussions on taking forward our partnership across trade, investments, connectivity, development partnership, and capacity building,' he wrote on X.
Earlier, addressing a gathering at the Adwa Memorial Museum in Addis Ababa on Friday, Jaishankar emphasised the need for India and Africa to strengthen their historic partnership, advance self-reliance and push for reforms in global institutions.
He said both sides shared developmental aspirations, historical experiences and a commitment to a more equitable global order, adding that their partnership must evolve to address contemporary challenges.
"India and Africa have developed a tradition of working hand in hand in international forums, and that continues to this day... Our relationship must evolve and keep pace with the times," he said.
Highlighting the development goals of both sides, Jaishankar said India was pursuing the vision of 'Viksit Bharat' by 2047, while Africa had outlined its aspirations through 'Agenda 2063'.
"Today, India is pursuing the goal of Viksit Bharat, or developed India, by 2047. We seek to transform ourselves by the centenary of our independence. Africa, likewise, has articulated its own vision through Agenda 2063, which outlines the Africa we want," he said.
The minister said India was Africa's fourth-largest trading partner, with bilateral trade turnover nearing USD 100 billion. Indian investments across the continent span manufacturing, telecommunications, pharmaceuticals, energy, mining, agriculture, infrastructure, financial services and information technology.
"We strongly encourage our businesses to view Africa as an investment destination of choice. Indian businesses, as a rule, have created local employment, encouraged value addition and strengthened African national economies," he said.
Jaishankar also called for fair representation of India and Africa in global decision-making, arguing that the existing international order did not adequately reflect their interests.
"India and Africa cannot remain unrepresented or underrepresented in global decision-making," he said.
He reiterated India's support for reforms to the United Nations Security Council, saying the current Council neither delivered effectively nor represented countries fairly.
Jaishankar also highlighted opportunities for cooperation in digital governance, including digital identity, payments, financial inclusion and public service delivery, as well as in space, drone technologies and artificial intelligence.
India and Africa share longstanding historical and cultural ties, shaped by trade across the Indian Ocean, shared experiences of colonialism and cooperation in international forums.
Jaishankar arrived in Ethiopia on Thursday as part of his three-nation African tour, which also included visits to Ghana and Cote d'Ivoire. (ANI)

Denmark allows citizens of nine countries to enter the country without a visa if they hold qualifying biometric passports, although the exemption is part of the country’s existing immigration rules rather than a newly announced policy.
The countries are Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Georgia, Kosovo, Moldova, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia and Ukraine, according to the Danish Immigration Service’s official visa guidance.
Full list of the 9 countries
According to the Danish Immigration Service, citizens of the following countries qualify for visa-free entry when they meet the applicable biometric passport requirements.
Albania: Citizens holding qualifying biometric passports are exempt from the visa requirement.
Bosnia and Herzegovina: Holders of biometric passports can enter Denmark without a visa.
Georgia: Biometric passport holders qualify, although the exemption does not cover diplomatic, service, official or special passports under the stated rules.
Kosovo: Citizens with biometric passports qualify for the exemption.

The event, which opened on Monday, October 12, is being held under the theme, “From Confidence to Capital: Unlocking the Next Wave of Growth through Strategic Investment.”
It forms part of the UK-Ghana Growth Partnership and follows the Ghana-UK Investment Summit held in London in June.
The roadshow is expected to showcase investment opportunities in sectors including agribusiness, pharmaceuticals and health technology, financial services, infrastructure and the circular economy.
Participants include Ghana’s High Commissioner to the United Kingdom, Sabah Zita Benson; Presidential Adviser on the 24-Hour Economy and Accelerated Export Development Programme (24H+), Augustus Goosie Tanoh; and Claire Innes, Deputy Director of the Growth Directorate at the UK’s Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO).
The event builds on the UK-Ghana Trade and Investment Summit organised by the UK-Ghana Chamber of Commerce in September, where investment matchmaking sessions generated interest in opportunities worth more than £250 million.
These opportunities form part of a broader investment pipeline exceeding £1.4 billion across several sectors, according to the organisers. Some are now progressing through discussions with prospective investors and strategic partners.
British High Commissioner to Ghana, Dr Christian Rogg, said the roadshow would help turn investor interest into concrete business opportunities and create jobs in both countries.
“The UK Investment Roadshow is the Growth Partnership in action, connecting UK investors with credible opportunities in Ghana and building on our strong momentum to unlock investment, create jobs and turn shared ambition into practical economic opportunities for both countries,” he said.
The event is taking place alongside AFSIC – Investing in Africa, an annual investment conference focused on African markets that is held outside the continent.
Executive Director of the UK-Ghana Chamber of Commerce, Adjoba Kyiamah, said the roadshow would help move discussions from investment interest to practical business deals.
“This strategic event represents an important next step in converting interest into action,” she said.
Kyiamah added that the event would provide a platform to showcase Ghana’s investment potential, facilitate business connections and advance commercially viable discussions with investors seeking opportunities in Africa.
The programme includes an Investment Opportunities Roundtable hosted by British Expertise International, a Ghana Country Investment Session at the AFSIC Summit and a Ghana Investor Deal Room Day.
The deal room will allow investors to engage directly with businesses, project sponsors and government representatives to discuss investment-ready projects.
The roadshow is being delivered by the UK-Ghana Chamber of Commerce and the UK Government’s Jobs and Economic Transformation (JET) programme in Ghana as part of efforts to deepen trade and investment ties between the two countries.

articles.title: Africa Is No Longer Asking to Be Seen. It Is Asking to Be Paid. - The Guardian Nigeria News
articles.summary: Africa Is No Longer Asking to Be Seen. It Is Asking to Be Paid.  The Guardian Nigeria News
articles.full_text:
From the global triumph of Nigerian music and film to the emerging institutions financing African creativity, a new economic argument is taking shape: recognition is no longer enough. The continent must own, trade and profit from what it creates.
There is a peculiar irony in Africa’s latest encounter with the world. Its music fills international arenas. Its fashion inspires global runways. Its films travel across streaming platforms. Its writers win prestigious prizes. Its cultural vocabulary, once dismissed as provincial, increasingly shapes the language of global popular culture.
Yet the continent that produces so much of this imagination still struggles to capture a proportionate share of its economic value.
The world has discovered that Africa is fashionable. Africa is beginning to ask a rather less fashionable question.
Who is collecting the money?
It is a question that reaches far beyond entertainment. It concerns trade, finance, intellectual property, institutional capacity and the unfinished business of economic independence.
For much of its modern history, Africa occupied a familiar position in international commerce. It supplied raw materials while other economies manufactured finished products, controlled distribution and accumulated much of the profit.
Today, the commodities are changing. Music, cinema, fashion, design and digital content are joining oil, cocoa, copper and gold as sources of international demand.
But an uncomfortable possibility remains: Africa could become a cultural superpower without becoming an equivalent economic power.
The distinction is fundamental.
Being admired is not the same as being wealthy. Being internationally visible is not the same as controlling the commercial infrastructure through which that visibility becomes income.
And nowhere is this contradiction more fascinating than in Nigeria.
The Country That Exported Its Imagination
In 1977, Lagos hosted FESTAC, the Second World Black and African Festival of Arts and Culture. It was an extraordinary declaration of African cultural confidence, bringing performers, intellectuals and artists from across Africa and its diaspora into a common celebration of Black identity.
Nigeria was then enjoying an oil boom. Petroleum revenues helped finance a festival that announced the country’s ambition to become a cultural centre of the Black world.
Nearly half a century later, Nigeria has achieved much of that ambition, although through circumstances its organisers could scarcely have imagined.
Afrobeats travels internationally without government sponsorship. Nollywood has cultivated audiences across continents. Nigerian fashion, comedy, literature and digital creativity circulate through markets that scarcely existed in 1977.
The transformation is remarkable because so much of it occurred despite persistent weaknesses in infrastructure, financing and public institutions.
Nigeria’s creative entrepreneurs improvised their own routes into international commerce.
They demonstrated that talent could flourish in difficult economic conditions. But they also exposed the limits of celebrating resilience as though it were an economic development strategy.
A country cannot build a globally competitive creative economy on ingenuity alone.
The question now is whether the institutions surrounding Nigerian creativity can become as sophisticated as the talent producing it.
The Economics Behind the Applause
The figures illustrate both the opportunity and the distance yet to travel.
According to the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry, recorded music revenues in sub-Saharan Africa increased by 15.2 per cent in 2025, reaching approximately $120 million.
It is an encouraging performance, but one that deserves context. South Africa accounted for more than three-quarters of the region’s recorded music revenues.
International enthusiasm for African music should therefore not be confused with the existence of a sufficiently developed commercial market throughout the continent.
An artist may accumulate millions of streams without possessing meaningful control over recording rights, publishing income or international licensing arrangements.
A successful filmmaker may reach a worldwide audience while surrendering significant future value through unfavourable distribution agreements.
A fashion designer may influence international aesthetics while lacking the capital, production capacity or trademark protection necessary to build a durable global brand.
There is nothing inherently objectionable about working with international labels, distributors, investors or streaming companies. Such relationships can provide vital expertise and market access.
The decisive question is whether African enterprises negotiate as owners of valuable assets or merely as suppliers of creative material.
The distinction is the creative economy’s equivalent of the old commodity problem.
Africa must avoid exporting imagination on terms that leave much of its enduring value elsewhere.
When Creativity Meets the Balance Sheet
Some Nigerian financial institutions are beginning to confront that challenge.
The Bank of Industry established its Creative Industry Group in 2011, recognising the sector as a legitimate area for development financing
Nigeria’s Export-Import Bank, NEXIM, also operates a Nigerian Creative and Entertainment Industry Loan Scheme covering music, film, television, fashion and related infrastructure.
One particularly significant feature of NEXIM’s documentation requirements is its recognition of intellectual property as potential collateral, subject to valuation.
That seemingly technical provision points towards a substantial economic transformation.
Traditional lenders are accustomed to financing assets they can readily value: land, machinery, buildings and inventories.
Creative enterprises frequently depend on less tangible assets, including copyrights, trademarks, music catalogues, distribution rights and commercially valuable brands.
If such assets can be properly valued, protected and financed, an entirely different investment ecosystem becomes possible.
The federal government’s Creative Economy Development Fund represents another attempt to improve financing for cultural and creative businesses.
Yet announced facilities and established schemes should not be mistaken for proof that financing has become widely accessible.
The more demanding questions concern disbursement, affordability, collateral requirements, repayment conditions and whether enterprises outside a narrow circle of established players can obtain funding.
A genuine creative economy requires more than capital availability on paper.
It requires financiers who understand the economics of intellectual property and entrepreneurs capable of presenting commercially credible businesses.
Bringing Creativity Into the Trading Economy
The growing engagement of business institutions offers another indication of change.
The Nigerian Association of Chambers of Commerce, Industry, Mines and Agriculture, NACCIMA, now has a Creative Economy Trade Group, reflecting an expanding recognition that creative activity belongs within the country’s organised commercial economy.
This is significant because chambers of commerce traditionally occupy territory associated with manufacturing, investment, industrial development and conventional trade.
Their increasing engagement with creative enterprise suggests a gradual shift in how the sector is understood.
The relationship is also becoming more international.
In March 2025, Nigeria and the United Kingdom launched a Creatives Working Group under their Enhanced Trade and Investment Partnership.
It was a recognition that cultural exchange must be accompanied by more structured discussions about enterprise development, commercial partnerships and market access.
Institutions such as the Lagos Chamber of Commerce and Industry and the Nigerian-British Chamber of Commerce can help create the connections through which creative businesses gain access to investors, professional services and established international commercial networks.
But institutional recognition must ultimately produce measurable commercial results.
The real achievement will come when a Nigerian production company can secure export financing as confidently as a manufacturer, or when a fashion enterprise can access regional distribution networks without depending entirely on informal arrangements.
Creative industries should no longer be treated as decorative additions to economic policy.
They are businesses, and they require the infrastructure of business.
A Different Kind of Festival
It is within this emerging conversation that Artistic Pulse Festival (APF) & Trade Fair 2026 offers an interesting Nigerian example.
Scheduled for November 26–29 at the Federal Palace Hotel in Lagos, the platform is being developed around the theme Creativity, Enterprise, Trade and Sustainable Growth.
Its proposition deliberately extends beyond the familiar festival model.
Alongside cultural programming, APF is designed to bring together businesses, creative entrepreneurs, investors, trade institutions, international delegations and potential commercial partners.
The planned activities include exhibitions, business-to-business engagement, investment discussions, cross-border partnerships and creative industry showcases.
That architecture is important.
Africa has no shortage of festivals demonstrating its artistic excellence. What it needs increasingly are platforms capable of connecting that excellence to contracts, financing, distribution and commercial relationships.
APF’s engagement with established business figures also illustrates the direction of travel. articles.title: Taiwan lifts visa ban on China-friendly Morocco after three-month standoff, but extends DR Congo restrictions by 90 days - Business Insider Africa
articles.summary: Taiwan lifts visa ban on China-friendly Morocco after three-month standoff, but extends DR Congo restrictions by 90 days  Business Insider Africa
articles.full_text:
- Taiwan has resumed visa processing for Moroccan nationals after Morocco restored visa services for Taiwanese citizens, ending a three-month dispute.
- The diplomatic dispute began when Morocco stopped processing visa confirmation letters for Taiwanese travelers, prompting reciprocal action by Taiwan.
- Taiwan also lifted health-related visa restrictions for Ugandan residents after an Ebola review, but extended similar restrictions for Democratic Republic of Congo residents until late November.
- These decisions reflect a combination of diplomatic reciprocity and public health concerns shaping Taiwan's visa policies towards African countries.
The decision, effective October 12, 2026, follows Morocco’s restoration of visa services for Taiwanese passport holders on September 21, ending a nearly three-month diplomatic dispute.
Meanwhile, Taiwan continues to review visa restrictions affecting other African countries, having restored access for Uganda while maintaining Ebola-related restrictions on the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).
Why Taiwan suspended Moroccan visas
The visa dispute began on July 23, when Morocco's embassy in Japan stopped processing visa confirmation letters for Taiwanese travellers without publicly explaining its decision.
According to Taiwan's Bureau of Consular Affairs, Taiwanese passport holders were ineligible for Morocco's electronic visas and had to obtain confirmation letters from Moroccan diplomatic missions before travelling.
In response, Taiwan suspended visa applications from Moroccan nationals on July 30, citing the principle of "reciprocity". The restrictions affected tourism and business travel, although exceptions remained available to applicants with special government approval.
The dispute began to ease on September 21, when Morocco resumed accepting visa confirmation letter applications from Taiwanese travellers.
However, the East Asian island, delayed lifting its restrictions while seeking clarification on whether Morocco's decision covered all travel purposes.
Following confirmation from Moroccan authorities, Taiwan announced that normal visa processing for Moroccan nationals would resume on October 12, 2026.
Uganda regains access as DR Congo restrictions continue
Taiwan has also lifted visa restrictions affecting Uganda, although those measures stemmed from public health concerns rather than diplomatic disagreements.
On June 2, 2026, Taiwanese authorities imposed a 90-day suspension on visa issuance and entry for residents of Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), citing Ebola-related health risks.
The restrictions included exemptions for diplomatic personnel, eligible students, certain family members of Taiwanese citizens and humanitarian emergencies.
Following a review of the health situation, Taiwan lifted the restrictions on Ugandan residents on August 28.
However, authorities extended the measures affecting DRC residents for another 90 days, until November 28, citing continued public health concerns.
One-China policy and Taiwan's relations with Africa
The visa developments come against the backdrop of Taiwan's limited diplomatic presence in Africa, where most countries, including Morocco, Uganda and the DRC, maintain formal relations with Beijing under the One-China principle.
In January 2026, the African Union reaffirmed its support for the principle, recognising the People's Republic of China as the sole legal government representing China and backing Beijing's claim over Taiwan.
Taiwan rejected the declaration, maintaining that it is not subordinate to Beijing.
Despite these diplomatic differences, African countries continue to engage with Taiwan on travel and other practical matters. Eswatini remains the only African country with formal diplomatic ties to Taiwan.

articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia's energy minister on Monday said the country had been tested but would mount a "serious" response after a string of attacks on Riyadh's international airport by Yemen's Houthis that left 18 people dead.
Lethal airport strikes since last week have rocked the world's top oil exporter, which is pursuing an expensive economic reform drive aimed at attracting foreign investment.
Yemen's civil war, where a Saudi-led military coalition supports the government against the Iran-backed Houthis, has reignited months into the US-Iran conflict that has roiled energy markets and plunged the Middle East into crisis.
"Energy security can't be taken for granted," Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman told an energy conference in Riyadh, as oil prices topped $105 a barrel.
"The events of recent weeks are serious, our response must be equally serious."
"For Saudi Arabia, these circumstances have tested our infrastructure, our institutions, our people, and our resilience," he added.
On Saturday, Houthi strikes killed 13 people and wounded hundreds at King Khalid International Airport -- the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in more than a decade.
Four people died in earlier attacks on Wednesday and Thursday, and another was killed on Sunday. Operations remained suspended at the sprawling airport on Riyadh's outskirts on Monday.
CCTV footage of Saturday's attack released by Saudi authorities showed Muslim pilgrims in religious attire waiting in departure lounges before a sudden flash tore through the building and brought down flaming debris.
- 'The whole house shook' -
The atmosphere in Riyadh remained tense on Monday, as state broadcaster Al Ekhbariya said the military coalition was responding to drone and missile threats, and Australia's embassy warned its citizens in the city to shelter in place.
The Houthis on Sunday claimed multiple attacks over the previous 24 hours, including on the airport, and threatened to keep targeting Saudi transit hubs, calling them "a theatre of operations for our forces".
Hours later, the coalition said yet another projectile had struck Riyadh airport, sparking a fire, while air defences intercepted a missile nearby.
AFP journalists and locals reported hearing multiple blasts in the capital on Sunday.
"The whole house shook," said one resident of the Al-Aarid neighbourhood in the city's north.
Riyadh's airport was not the only one to suffer a deadly attack: early on Monday, officials said one person had been killed and 11 wounded in a strike on Dammam airport.
The Saudi-led coalition said Monday that it had also "intercepted and destroyed" a Houthi ballistic missile heading for the southern city of Khamis Mushait, home to a major military base.
Riyadh hosts a packed calendar of events at this time of year, including its flagship Future Investment Initiative conference, which draws foreign leaders and business titans.
- 'Full-fledged war crime' -
Despite vast spending on military hardware, the Houthi attacks on oil, military and transport facilities across the large, mostly desert country are stretching Saudi defences.
"Saudi air defences have been able to intercept some Houthi missile and drone attacks, but Saudi Arabia is so large that it's simply impossible for them to consistently defend themselves," said Thomas Juneau, security analyst at Ottawa University.
The anti-Houthi coalition called Saturday's attack a "full-fledged war crime" and vowed to "respond decisively".
The attack drew condemnation from the United Nations and leaders including US President Donald Trump, who said he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis.
Iran, which backs the Houthis, said Monday it was "deeply concerned" over the recent escalation.
Witnesses to Saturday's strike described chaos in the aftermath.
"Some had lost a hand or an arm. People were running while carrying injured people, covered in blood," a 32-year-old Riyadh resident told AFP.
Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that has supported Yemen's government militarily since 2015, including by seeking to exert control over Yemeni airspace and the airport in the Houthi-held capital Sanaa.
Ottawa University's Juneau said the Houthis now "want to do to Saudi Arabia what Saudi Arabia does to them".

From MeTL and Bakhresa to NMB, CRDB, Vodacom, Barrick and Selcom, these 25 executives sit over companies, assets and financial infrastructure whose decisions influence investment, credit, exports, employment and everyday commerce across Tanzania.
Tanzania’s private economy is becoming large enough for decisions made inside a relatively small number of companies to carry national consequences. A lending decision at NMB or CRDB can determine whether a manufacturer expands. Capital expenditure by Vodacom, Yas or Airtel affects the infrastructure through which millions of Tanzanians communicate, access the internet and move money. Production decisions by cement, steel and beverage manufacturers move through construction, agriculture, logistics and retail. Investment decisions at Geita, North Mara and Bulyanhulu feed directly into exports, foreign exchange earnings, tax revenue and government dividends.
Uchumi360 identified 25 executives whose positions in 2026 place them over companies, assets or financial infrastructure with an unusually large transmission into the wider Tanzanian economy.
This is not a ranking of personal wealth, public visibility or corporate seniority. Founder ownership alone is insufficient, and neither is a chief executive title. The selection considers the scale of the institution an executive controls, the economic sectors it touches, the capital it allocates, the suppliers and workers dependent on it, and the extent to which decisions made inside that organisation can affect investment, credit, employment, exports, tax revenue, infrastructure or household consumption.
The list consequently includes different forms of corporate power. Mohammed Dewji and the Bakhresa family represent locally accumulated industrial capital. Ruth Zaipuna and Abdulmajid Nsekela lead two of the country’s most consequential pools of commercial credit. Philip Besiimire, Pierre Canton Bacara and Charles Kamoto operate communications infrastructure that increasingly doubles as financial infrastructure. Mining executives control some of Tanzania’s largest export generating assets, while manufacturers in cement, steel, beverages and consumer goods sit inside supply chains extending from farms and factories to thousands of wholesalers and retailers.
Banking has a large presence for a structural reason. Tanzania’s capital market remains relatively shallow compared with the financing needs of the economy, leaving commercial banks responsible for much of the credit required by companies, households, traders and major projects. Who controls bank capital therefore matters disproportionately.
1. Mohammed Dewji, Chief Executive Officer, MeTL Group
Mohammed Dewji leads one of the largest privately owned industrial groups headquartered in Tanzania. MeTL has evolved from a trading business into a diversified manufacturer operating across food processing, edible oils, beverages, textiles, agriculture, logistics, consumer goods and other industries. Dewji said in 2026 that the group manufactures more than 50 product categories, operates in 11 African countries, employs more than 40,000 people and is on course to generate more than US$3 billion in annual revenue.
Its significance comes from the number of economic layers contained inside one Tanzanian owned group. MeTL buys agricultural commodities, processes raw materials, manufactures finished goods, moves them through its logistics operations and distributes them into consumer markets. Dewji is also pushing the company further into resource processing, including graphite, extending the group from traditional manufacturing towards minerals linked to batteries and the global energy transition. Few domestically controlled companies influence as many parts of Tanzania’s productive economy at once.
2. Abubakar Said Salim Bakhresa, Managing Director, Said Salim Bakhresa & Company Limited
Abubakar Said Salim Bakhresa represents the second generation of executive leadership inside one of Tanzania’s largest homegrown industrial groups. He is Managing Director of Said Salim Bakhresa & Company Limited, the flagship business of Bakhresa Group, while also holding leadership responsibilities across the group’s grain milling, sugar, media and regional businesses. Bakhresa Group reports annual turnover exceeding US$800 million and direct employment of more than 8,000 people.
The economic weight behind those figures is found in the supply chain. Bakhresa businesses connect grain imports and domestic agriculture with milling, food production, beverages, sugar, packaging, logistics, broadcasting and distribution. Its Azam businesses have also expanded the group’s presence beyond Tanzania into several African markets. Abubakar Bakhresa therefore sits over a company whose decisions affect food manufacturing, regional trade and the cost and availability of products consumed by millions of households.
3. Ruth Zaipuna, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer, NMB Bank
Ruth Zaipuna has led NMB Bank since 2020 and became a director of the bank in 2025. NMB describes her as its Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer, placing her at the head of one of Tanzania’s largest commercial banks.
The importance of that position is ultimately about capital allocation. NMB provides financing across retail banking, agriculture, small businesses, large corporates, trade and public sector activity. Decisions over which sectors receive credit, on what terms and at what scale influence business expansion far beyond the bank itself. In an economy where bank lending remains a primary source of external finance for companies, Zaipuna controls one of the most consequential channels connecting deposits and institutional capital to productive investment.
4. Dr Abdulmajid Nsekela, Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director, CRDB Bank
Dr Abdulmajid Nsekela leads CRDB Bank as Group Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director. Under his leadership, CRDB has combined its large domestic banking operation with expansion elsewhere in East and Central Africa, giving Tanzania one of its clearest examples of a home headquartered financial institution developing into a regional business.
CRDB’s influence inside Tanzania comes from the breadth of borrowers and transactions it finances. The bank operates across corporate banking, agriculture, trade, retail finance, small businesses, infrastructure and institutional banking. Its growing regional presence adds another dimension: Tanzanian banking capital is increasingly participating in markets beyond the country’s borders. Nsekela therefore sits at the intersection of domestic credit allocation and Tanzania’s emerging export of financial services.

NBC’s significance comes from its presence across corporate, commercial, retail and institutional finance. Large companies require working capital, trade finance, foreign exchange services and investment funding, while smaller businesses depend on banking relationships that determine whether they can purchase equipment, build inventory or expand to new markets. Sabi occupies an important position within that flow of credit, particularly as competition among Tanzania’s major banks intensifies around corporate finance, transaction banking and digital services.

Transactions involving infrastructure, large corporate borrowing, structured finance, trade and foreign investment frequently require institutions able to connect domestic borrowers with capital beyond Tanzania. Rwegasira therefore operates close to some of the largest financing decisions in the economy, particularly where local investment intersects with international capital.

Laizer’s influence is therefore less about the size of Absa alone than its position as one of the institutions through which Tanzanian businesses interact with regional financial markets. articles.title: Why Falling Inflation Does Not Mean Lower Living Costs in Egypt - Sada Elbalad English
articles.summary: Why Falling Inflation Does Not Mean Lower Living Costs in Egypt  Sada Elbalad English
articles.full_text:
Egypt's annual inflation rate has continued to decline, but the improvement has yet to translate into meaningful financial relief for many households, as rising food prices, transport costs, housing expenses and pressure on purchasing power continue to strain family budgets.
Official figures released on October 10 showed that annual urban inflation eased to 13.9% in September 2026, down from 14.5% in August. However, consumer prices increased by 1.3% during September alone, their fastest monthly rise since May.
The contrast raises a central question: why do Egyptians continue to face mounting living costs when inflation is falling?
Why Lower Inflation Does Not Mean Lower Prices
The explanation lies in the difference between inflation and actual price levels.
A declining inflation rate does not necessarily mean goods and services are becoming cheaper. It means prices are increasing more slowly than before.
For example, a typical basket of goods costing EGP 1,000 in September 2025 would cost approximately EGP 1,139 a year later if its prices followed the overall urban inflation index.
September's annual slowdown also reflected a statistical effect. Consumer prices had increased sharply in September 2025, creating a higher comparison base that helped reduce this year's annual rate.
Meanwhile, nationwide inflation, which covers a broader geographical area, actually edged up to 12.8% in September from 12.7% in August.
Food, Transport and Housing Drive Household Pressure
Food remains among the most visible sources of financial pressure.
Urban food and beverage prices increased by 2.8% in September, reversing three consecutive months of declines. Vegetable prices surged 14.7%, while meat and poultry rose 2.2%.
For families purchasing groceries daily or weekly, such increases can outweigh the significance of a lower national inflation reading.
Housing presents an even greater challenge.
Annual inflation in housing and utilities reached 35.2% in September, despite slowing from 42.8% in August. Actual rents increased by 0.9% during the month.
Transport costs were 24.3% higher than a year earlier, while education expenses increased by 18.7%.
Egypt also raised domestic fuel prices by approximately 14% to 17% in March 2026, adding pressure on motorists, transport operators and businesses dependent on deliveries.
Together, these expenses consume a substantial proportion of household income, leaving less money available for savings and discretionary purchases.
Economists Warn of Continued Pressure
Heba Monir, an economist at HC Securities, had correctly forecast September's 1.3% monthly inflation increase, although food prices proved a stronger driver than she anticipated.
According to analysis published by EnterpriseAM, Monir expects monthly inflation to accelerate to approximately 2.1% in October, partly because of anticipated fuel price increases.
Hany Genena, an economist at Ahly Pharos, has also warned that annual inflation could rise to between 16% and 16.5% during the final quarter of 2026.
These remain forecasts rather than confirmed outcomes.
The longer-term damage to purchasing power is another concern.
World Bank estimates indicate that poverty, measured against the international benchmark for lower-middle-income countries, increased by approximately five percentage points between 2022 and 2024.
Although Egypt has increased minimum wages and expanded social protection measures, households whose earnings have not matched cumulative price increases continue to face reduced purchasing power.
The World Bank has warned that inflation remains a significant obstacle to poverty reduction, despite improvements in broader economic indicators.
For households, meaningful relief will depend not simply on lower annual inflation figures, but on sustained price stability, higher real incomes and slower increases in unavoidable expenses such as food, rent, utilities and transport.

articles.title: Global economic fragmentation and implications for Africa and Nigeria - TheCable
articles.summary: Global economic fragmentation and implications for Africa and Nigeria  TheCable
articles.full_text:
BY OLUFEMI ADUWO
The 2026 World Bank-IMF Annual Meetings in Thailand take place against a backdrop of geopolitical rivalry, protectionist trade policies, technological disruption, mounting sovereign debt and financial uncertainty. For Africa and Nigeria, these developments are not remote questions of international economics. They will shape trade competitiveness, investment flows, employment, fiscal capacity and the prospects for sustainable development.
The central challenge is to turn global economic turbulence into opportunities for industrial growth while reducing exposure to external shocks. Six interconnected issues warrant particular attention.
Global economic fragmentation reflects the erosion of international economic integration under pressure from geopolitical competition, sanctions and the reconfiguration of supply chains. As major economies prioritise strategic autonomy, international commerce increasingly reflects political alignments alongside comparative advantage.
For Africa, this shift presents both risks and opportunities. Supply-chain diversification could attract investment into manufacturing, mineral processing, energy and agro-industrial production. However, commodity-price volatility, weaker external demand and restricted access to technology could deepen existing vulnerabilities. Economies dependent on exporting unprocessed commodities remain particularly exposed to decisions made beyond their borders.
Nigeria must therefore reduce its dependence on crude-oil exports by expanding petrochemicals, gas processing, agro-industry, mineral beneficiation and export-oriented manufacturing. Reliable electricity, efficient logistics and predictable regulation are essential to this transition. The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) also offers an opportunity to expand regional value chains, strengthen intra-African trade and improve the continent’s bargaining position in global markets.
Protectionism compounds these challenges. Tariffs, import restrictions, subsidies and non-tariff barriers can distort competition, raise production costs and provoke retaliation. For African exporters, restricted market access could undermine industrial growth and limit opportunities to diversify exports.
Nigeria should resist indiscriminate import substitution. Selective protection may be justified where it supports industries capable of becoming internationally competitive, but such measures should be temporary, transparent and tied to measurable productivity targets. Industrial policy must expand productive efficiency rather than shelter inefficient enterprises indefinitely.
Artificial intelligence presents another structural challenge. Automation, predictive analytics and machine learning can improve productivity, accelerate scientific research and transform public services. Yet the benefits will not be distributed equally. Countries with inadequate digital infrastructure, limited computing capacity and shortages of skilled workers risk falling further behind.
Nigeria could apply AI in agriculture, medical diagnostics, financial services, public administration and education. Realising these benefits, however, requires dependable electricity, affordable connectivity and widespread digital literacy. Investment in science, technology, engineering and mathematics, vocational training and teacher development must accompany stronger collaboration among universities, research institutions and businesses. Policymakers must also address occupational displacement, data protection and unequal access to emerging technologies.
Debt sustainability is equally important. Governments need financing for infrastructure, healthcare, education, climate adaptation and social protection, yet rising borrowing costs and weak revenue mobilisation constrain their capacity to invest. For Nigeria, the central concern is not simply the ratio of public debt to gross domestic product, but also the proportion of government revenue consumed by debt servicing. A narrow revenue base leaves the country particularly vulnerable to fiscal pressure.
Strengthening domestic revenue mobilisation, improving expenditure discipline, ensuring transparent borrowing and applying rigorous project appraisal are therefore essential. Borrowing should prioritise investments that expand productive capacity and generate future economic returns rather than routinely finance recurrent expenditure. Equally, macroeconomic adjustment must be assessed against its consequences for household welfare, including food affordability, purchasing power and access to essential services.
Mobilising private capital can help bridge Africa’s infrastructure and investment gaps. However, investors require predictable regulation, enforceable contracts, credible institutions and effective security arrangements. Currency volatility and uncertainty over project revenues can also make long-term investment prohibitively expensive.
Public-private partnerships must consequently be transparent, commercially viable and subject to effective oversight. Development finance institutions can use guarantees, blended finance and carefully structured risk-sharing arrangements to attract private investors, while domestic pension funds and insurers can provide additional long-term capital where appropriate safeguards exist. The overriding objective should be to finance projects that generate sustainable returns, create employment and strengthen local supply chains.
Financial stability underpins these ambitions. Capital outflows, exchange-rate depreciation, volatile interest rates, banking-sector vulnerabilities and cyberattacks can disrupt investment and raise import costs. Nigeria needs coherent fiscal and monetary policies, effective financial supervision and robust risk management to contain these pressures. Beyond national reforms, deeper African capital markets, regional financial cooperation and more efficient cross-border payment systems could improve the continent’s capacity to withstand external shocks.
These challenges ultimately converge on the need for stronger economic institutions and a more diversified productive base. Fragmentation calls for greater resilience; protectionism demands export competitiveness; artificial intelligence requires investment in human capital; debt sustainability depends on fiscal capacity; private investment requires credible institutions; and financial stability rests on sound economic management.
Nigeria must pursue these priorities through a coherent strategy that measures progress not only by GDP growth, inflation, exchange-rate movements and fiscal balances, but also by productivity, employment, real household incomes and poverty reduction. Economic reforms should be judged by whether they improve the capacity of businesses to produce, workers to earn and households to maintain a decent standard of living.
The World Bank and IMF must, in turn, recognise that development requires more than macroeconomic adjustment. African economies need access to long-term financing, technology and fairer international markets. External support should complement, rather than replace, domestic accountability and sound economic governance.
Ultimately, Africa cannot secure economic sovereignty by withdrawing from global markets, nor can Nigeria achieve lasting prosperity through financial stabilisation alone. Both must become more productive, innovative and competitive while building the fiscal capacity to finance their development. The decisive test of the Bangkok deliberations will be whether international economic cooperation translates into stronger economies and measurable improvements in the living standards of ordinary citizens.

articles.full_text:
By Godwin Oritse
The Nigerian Ports Authority (NPA) has moved to address rail connectivity and logistics challenges affecting inland dry ports as part of efforts to integrate the facilities into the nation’s port system and improve cargo movement across the country.
The move followed a meeting between the NPA management, led by its Managing Director, Dr Abubakar Dantsoho, and the Executive Director of Dala Inland Dry Port, Mr Ahmad Rabiu, alongside representatives of Funtua Inland Dry Port, at the authority’s corporate headquarters in Marina, Lagos.
The engagement came after the Minister of Marine and Blue Economy, Dr Adegboyega Oyetola, directed the transfer of operational oversight of inland dry ports to the NPA.
The discussions focused on strengthening institutional collaboration, addressing infrastructure constraints and improving operational efficiency across Nigeria’s maritime logistics chain.
Speaking during the meeting, Dantsoho stressed the need to upgrade inland dry port infrastructure and technical capacity to complement ongoing modernisation efforts at the nation’s seaports.
He said the facilities must be equipped to handle increasing cargo volumes and support the broader transformation of Nigeria’s maritime sector.
“For our Inland Dry Ports to function at the same velocity as the ongoing modernisation across our seaports, we must proactively upgrade dry port infrastructure and technical capacity,” Dantsoho said.
He explained that the integration of digital platforms, including the Port Community System (PCS) and the National Single Window, into seaport operations must be matched by corresponding improvements at inland dry ports.
“As we integrate digital systems such as the Port Community System (PCS) and the National Single Window in our seaports, the dry ports must deploy modern equipment and advanced technical capabilities to handle larger cargo volumes and bigger vessels coming to our coast,” he added.
The NPA managing director also called for increased private-sector investment in inland dry port infrastructure, noting that stronger investment would be critical to improving cargo handling capacity and operational efficiency.
He cited APM Terminals’ establishment of an Export Processing Terminal in Northern Nigeria as an example of private-sector participation in the development of inland logistics infrastructure.
Dantsoho assured stakeholders that efforts to optimise the inland port system were underway and confirmed plans to visit the Dala and Funtua facilities to assess their operational conditions and infrastructure requirements.
Speaking on behalf of the delegation, Hassan Bello welcomed the transfer of operational oversight to the NPA, expressing appreciation for what he described as a seamless transition.
Bello referenced the gazetted Port Act, which recognises inland dry ports as official ports of origin and destination, while drawing attention to challenges confronting the facilities, particularly inadequate rail connectivity and broader logistics constraints.
Rail access is a critical component of inland dry port operations, as efficient connections to the national rail network can facilitate cargo movement between seaports and inland destinations, potentially reducing pressure on road transport and lowering logistics costs.
The meeting also established a framework for further technical consultations, infrastructure integration and physical planning to identify the requirements for improving operations at the facilities.
The discussions highlighted the need for detailed technical assessments, stakeholder coordination and physical inspections to establish infrastructure priorities and guide subsequent project development.
The planned visits to Dala and Funtua inland dry ports are expected to provide the NPA with a clearer understanding of the facilities’ operational challenges and the interventions required to strengthen their roles in cargo distribution, trade facilitation and Nigeria’s wider maritime logistics network.

articles.title: Nigeria targets aircraft-materials market with $362 million titanium project and US-built processing plant - Business Insider Africa
articles.summary: Nigeria targets aircraft-materials market with $362 million titanium project and US-built processing plant  Business Insider AfricaOndo Signs $362m Deal for Titanium Processing Plant  MSME Africa
articles.full_text:
- Ondo State has signed a partnership with PyVee for a proposed $362 million titanium-processing complex.
- The programme will begin with a $12 million pilot plant targeted for operation within approximately 21 months.
- An American partner is expected to fabricate the modular plant for installation in Nigeria.
- The state is contributing land for an equity stake, while full financing arrangements remain undisclosed.
The partnership with Nigerian company PyVee Limited would establish the facility in Ilaje, a coastal area of south-western Nigeria.
Development will begin with a $12 million commercial pilot plant. PyVee expects the initial facility to start operating approximately 21 months after the agreement, before expansion into a full-scale processing complex.
The state has allocated just over 100 hectares for the project and will receive shares in the venture in exchange for the land. Its ownership percentage has not been disclosed.
According to BusinessDay’s report, published on 10 October, the plant will process ilmenite into titanium dioxide pigment and titanium sponge. A US fabrication partner is expected to manufacture the modular plant before shipment to Nigeria for installation.
From mineral ore to industrial materials
The planned products serve different markets.
Titanium dioxide pigment is widely used in paints, plastics and paper. Titanium sponge is used to manufacture titanium metal, which has applications in aircraft, armour, marine equipment and medical implants.
Titanium’s strength relative to its weight and resistance to corrosion make it useful in aircraft manufacturing. The US Geological Survey identifies aerospace as the leading application for titanium metal in the United States.
For Nigeria, processing ilmenite locally would create an opportunity to sell industrial products rather than relying on exports of unprocessed minerals.
The proposed connection to aerospace and defence remains a commercial ambition. The announcement does not identify an aircraft manufacturer or defence company that has contracted to purchase the plant’s output.
Ondo takes a stake
The development will operate through PyVee Nigeria Titanium Limited, a joint-venture company.
Ondo’s land contribution makes the state a shareholder whose returns would depend on the business’s performance. The government will also support approvals, infrastructure and engagement with surrounding communities.
The project site was selected for access to lagoon water and gas infrastructure, alongside potential links to proposed port facilities and the Lagos–Calabar coastal corridor.
That arrangement gives the state a continuing financial interest in the facility, although the value of its land contribution and the terms governing its shares have not been made public.
A $12 million first step
The pilot plant is the immediate priority. It would precede the substantially larger investment needed for the full-scale complex.
The $362 million figure is an estimated development cost across the programme. Public reporting does not identify committed lenders or confirm that all the financing has been secured.
The American fabrication role is also distinct from US government investment. No American government funding or military procurement contract has been announced.
The project’s first test will therefore be whether PyVee can finance, construct and operate the pilot. Its wider significance would come from turning Nigerian mineral resources into a reliable source of processed materials for industrial buyers.

articles.title: PM Modi Launches ₹13,000 Crore Projects in Chennai, Spotlights VOC Port Mega Container Hub - Maritime Gateway
articles.summary: PM Modi Launches ₹13,000 Crore Projects in Chennai, Spotlights VOC Port Mega Container Hub  Maritime Gateway
articles.full_text:
Summary
Prime Minister Narendra Modi launched development projects worth over ₹13,000 crore in Chennai on October 11, spanning metro rail, railways, roads and industry. Highlighting port-led growth, he pointed to the roughly ₹17,000 crore plan to turn Thoothukudi’s VOC Port into a world-class mega container and green energy hub capable of handling ultra-large container ships.
Article
Chennai: Prime Minister Narendra Modi laid foundation stones for, inaugurated and dedicated to the nation development projects worth over ₹13,000 crore in Chennai on Saturday, October 11, 2026, while underlining the government’s push to develop a VOC Port mega container hub in Thoothukudi as part of a wider upgrade of India’s maritime infrastructure.
The Prime Minister said the projects, a mix of completed works and new developments, would ease daily commuting, boost industry and trade and create jobs for the state’s youth.
What did the Prime Minister say about ports?
Modi said port infrastructure across India is being strengthened to take the shipping sector to new heights, with Tamil Nadu playing a central role. He cited a recent decision to invest about ₹17,000 crore to transform V.O. Chidambaranar (VOC) Port into a world-class mega container and green energy hub that can accommodate ultra-large container vessels. “This will help Tamil Nadu become a global hub for industry and transport,” he said.
He added that ship turnaround times at Indian ports have been cut by half, helping Indian products reach global markets faster.
What is the VOC Port project?
The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs reportedly approved a ₹17,167 crore project at VOC Port last month to build a new outer harbour and expand container terminal capacity. About ₹11,733 crore is earmarked for works under the Hybrid Annuity Model, while ₹5,434 crore will fund container terminal construction on a Design-Build-Finance-Operate-Transfer basis.
The project aims to reduce dependence on foreign transshipment hubs, especially Colombo, which handles about 65% of containers from Thoothukudi. VOC Port currently accounts for around 7% of India’s container traffic.
VOC Port has also been positioning itself as a green energy hub. It became the first Indian port to produce green hydrogen through a pilot facility, and work is under way on a 750 cubic metre green methanol bunkering and refuelling facility linked to the proposed Kandla-Tuticorin green shipping corridor.
Which projects were launched?
Ahead of the visit, officials said the Prime Minister would open the 14.6-km Poonamallee-Vadapalani stretch, the first section of Chennai Metro’s Phase II, and inaugurate Amrit Bharat stations at Palani, Paramakudi, Namakkal, Ambasamudram and Vellore Cantonment, along with ₹700 crore of rail projects in Coimbatore.
Modi also laid the foundation stone for an advanced lubricant base oil project, which he said would create jobs and help reduce India’s imports. He earlier visited the Brain Research Centre at IIT Madras.
What did he say about metro and manufacturing?
Modi said metro services have expanded from five cities in 2014 to 25 today, with the network growing from about 250 km to more than 1,100 km.
On manufacturing, he said India has become the world’s second-largest mobile phone maker, with electronics exports up elevenfold since 2014, defence exports up fiftyfold and engineering exports at record levels. He stressed that strong manufacturing needs high-quality roads, railways and ports to move raw materials and finished goods efficiently.
What support was announced for fishermen?
The Prime Minister said thousands of crores have been approved for Tamil Nadu under the PM Matsya Sampada Yojana and other schemes to upgrade fishing harbours, build landing centres and improve cold chains. He cited the modernisation of Chennai Fishing Harbour, a seaweed park in the state and easier working capital for fishermen through Kisan Credit Cards, noting that India’s seafood exports hit record levels in both volume and value last year.
What is the wider significance?
The visit came as Modi marked 25 years as head of government. He said he would work with Chief Minister Joseph Vijay to advance Tamil Nadu’s development, calling for a “Viksit Bharat” through a “Viksit Tamil Nadu.”
For the maritime sector, the focus on VOC Port signals the Centre’s intent to build domestic transshipment capacity on the east coast and capture cargo that currently moves through foreign hubs.
FAQs
How much were the projects launched in Chennai worth?
The projects launched by Prime Minister Modi on October 11, 2026, were worth over ₹13,000 crore.
What is planned for VOC Port in Thoothukudi?
The government plans to invest about ₹17,000 crore to develop VOC Port into a mega container and green energy hub with a new outer harbour for ultra-large container ships.
Why is the VOC Port expansion important?
It aims to cut reliance on foreign transshipment hubs such as Colombo, which handles about 65% of Thoothukudi’s containers.
Which Chennai Metro stretch was opened?
The 14.6-km Poonamallee-Vadapalani stretch, the first section of Chennai Metro’s Phase II, was scheduled for inauguration.
What support did the PM mention for fishermen?
He cited PM Matsya Sampada Yojana funding, Chennai Fishing Harbour modernisation, a seaweed park and Kisan Credit Card access for fishermen.
